title: The Blog Post That Set the AI World on Fire
excerpt: For the past 24 hours, Silicon Valley has been obsessed with a 26,000-word blog post by the AI researcher Nick Cammarata
body: For the past 24 hours, Silicon Valley has been obsessed with a 26,000-word blog post by the AI researcher Nick Cammarata
The document has been called the “the most important essay,” “the most important result,” and “the single best piece of news” of the year , or in the history of AI research—or, perhaps, ever
Cammarata makes a series of bold, almost astonishing claims about the nature of AI that, if true, would upend some of his industry’s basic assumptions about the very thing it is building

And after months of AI-hacking sprees and mounting public backlash against the industry, many people see Cammarata as offering a glimmer of hope when it comes to not just understanding but also controlling the technology being unleashed on the world

Boiled down, Cammarata’s main contention is that generative-AI models are not actually black boxes, contrary to the common perception that these systems are so big and labyrinthine as to be nearly impenetrable
In fact, Cammarata argues, there is a relatively clear path toward understanding them

If that’s the case, the material significance could be tremendous: It would provide a way to map AI models’ inner workings and, in turn, perhaps prevent them from wreaking all sorts of harm—autonomously hacking companies and sovereign nations, encouraging users’ delusions, appearing to deceive AI researchers themselves
There is an entire field of research, called “mechanistic interpretability,” devoted to the study of just this
The argument is just as important as the person making it
Cammarata, a former OpenAI employee, is a respected figure in his field

Years ago, he played a key role in establishing the opposite claim, which is now common wisdom: that neural networks, the software architecture that generative AI is built on, are impossible, or at least very difficult, to understand

In this new essay, Cammarata, who now works at the AI-research company Goodfire, essentially says that he and his entire field have been wrong ever since. “The claims here are viscerally shocking,” one observer wrote

Or, as another wrote on X, they are “big big big big.” [ Read: Imagine every AI agent on Earth buying the same cheap paper towels ] Neural networks, inspired by the human brain, consist of layered connections among individual nodes, or “neurons,” that activate and send information to one another when responding to a query

Earlier research, including Cammarata’s, established that individual machine neurons can activate in response to many different, unrelated topics—for instance, one neuron can correspond to images of cat faces, cat legs, and the front of cars
Nobody was sure why this happened, but one explanation was that, because AI models contain far more information than they have neurons, they have to repurpose these nodes
Regardless, the basic units of an AI model having seemingly arbitrary, multitudinous functions would make it very difficult to understand what is going on under the hood
Cammarata now thinks that individual neurons can be understood and that each has a self-consistent function

Neural networks are not “tangled knots,” he wrote, but “clean.” He found that the cat-face and car-face neuron, for instance, was actually responding to things with a V-shape—including V-shaped flames and jets of water
This would make AI’s internal mechanisms relatively straightforward and predictable rather than mysterious and nebulous

And if we can harness that understanding, some people in the industry believe, AI will be much less likely to go haywire and, say, kill us all. “This is truly one of the greatest cases for optimism in years!” the OpenAI researcher Adam Majmudar wrote on X
For one, his 26,000 words were merely a “working hypothesis” for a “forthcoming technical paper” and were thus hard, on a technical level, to evaluate
And the neural networks he studied most closely were vision models, which are generally simpler and better understood than the language models underlying ChatGPT and Claude
Cammarata could be mistaken, or he could be overstating his case
The blog post isn’t peer-reviewed, and the forthcoming paper probably won’t be, either, as is typical in the field

The research itself is something of a black box. (Cammarata, who did not immediately respond to a request for comment, wrote on X earlier today that he appreciates all of the discussion and that his approach “seems promising so far” for “bigger modern language models.”) Discussions of Cammarata’s essay have revealed philosophical rifts. “This is interesting work, but I don’t think it’s a significant update to the big picture,” Neel Nanda, who leads mechanistic interpretability at Google DeepMind, wrote in his appraisal of Cammarata’s findings
Even if researchers could approximate the function of every neuron in Claude Mythos 5.1 or GPT-6 Astra, that’s not the same as understanding how they connect and how the network works as a whole

Physicists have good models of atoms and interatomic interactions, but they cannot from first principles explain or predict every physical event (hence unpredictable extreme weather or, for that matter, the notion of free will)
You know all of your friends from school, various workplaces, and the local softball league, but you can’t always know whether they’ll get along at your birthday party
More to the point, insights into the inner workings of an AI model will not necessarily produce insights into how to make the technology more reliable
Interpretability may be necessary to build safer AI models, but it is by no means sufficient
If generative-AI models are actually legible under the hood, that would undoubtedly help make the technology safer

But many people in Silicon Valley, and especially employees at OpenAI, are discussing Cammarata’s blog post with a breathless enthusiasm that echoes Silicon Valley’s long track record of easy technical solutions and grand promises—an attitude that belies its mixed record on following through
Any research finding that pertains to AI safety will require an industry chasing multitrillion-dollar public offerings to slow down and take a long, hard look at itself

Perhaps even more concerning than an unintelligible superintelligence is the fact that a group of companies openly state that they don’t really know what they are building—and then continue to push that technology to extremes anyway
If Cammarata is correct, AI companies will have to work with one another, outside auditors, and governments to figure out how to translate such a breakthrough into safe and reliable products
And right now, absent any serious regulation, nobody can decide to take such action other than the companies themselves
All of which suggests that the real black boxes are OpenAI and Anthropic themselves.

title: Five Fabulous Days of Katie Zacharia
excerpt: The world will little note, nor long remember, the Katie Zacharia era
body: The world will little note, nor long remember, the Katie Zacharia era
Indeed, the tenure of the second White House press secretary of Donald Trump’s second term, which ended after five days and a single, 14-minute press conference, is already receding into memory

Yet what matters more than her press-secretarial contributions, or the ideas she stood for, is the period Zacharia represents: the Trump administration’s reversion to the hapless chaos of the president’s first term

Trump’s initial go-round was primarily a farce, setting bumbling aides against challenges such as finding the light switches in the Cabinet room, hurling burgers against the White House wall, and booking the wrong Four Seasons
Trump cycled through personnel like Spinal Tap drummers, as one hired helper after the next left in frustration or shame
The second term has operated with, if not normality, at least comparative efficiency

Chief of Staff Susie Wiles turned the executive branch from an exploding fireworks factory into a machine relentlessly processing the president’s whims into law. [ Read: Trump’s secret points system for Cabinet members ] Yet as the midterm elections draw near, the machine has begun to sputter

In the span of days, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced he would livestream a public execution, only for Trump to overrule him; the administration fired Kimberly Guilfoyle, its ambassador to Greece, for engaging in corruption so overt, it embarrassed even the most corrupt administration in history; and Politico reported that Trump is asking his friends what they think of Wiles, which is historically the prelude to his turning on an underling
In the midst of this multicar pileup, Zacharia briefly stepped forward as the administration’s stammering face
If you have ever felt awkward in a public setting, her single press conference was the stuff of recurrent nightmares
Zacharia read from the podium, head down, in the tone of a third-grade book report delivered verbally in front of the entire school by a child with crippling anxiety
She had to pause multiple times to take gulps of air
Trump, she said in one typical segment, “had a historic one-day war, and now we are, have a booming economy, and a great relationship”—here she stopped to catch herself—“with Venezuela

The U.S. achieved record domestic oil and gas production in 2025 and record crude and petroleum product exports in 2026.” At another point, attempting to discuss nuclear-power plants, she called them “something President Trump is delivering on, just like he delivers on every promise.” (Pause, gasp for breath.) “In addition to that, it, we will be, it, we will be, there is $54 billion tied to the Alaska LNG pipeline.” Then she told the assembled reporters, “My goal is to be able to communicate that in complete tandem with the president, as he is his own best spokesperson, and will absolutely be leading the way as—with that.” It was as if the notion that Trump could do her job much better than she could had intruded into her thoughts and made its way out of her mouth

She wrapped up the press conference after answering only three questions. [ Tom Nichols: Kimberly Guilfoyle broke Trump’s most important rule ] Shortly after, she appeared with the president on the White House lawn, and when a reporter asked which state’s bar exam she had passed—Zacharia has described herself as an attorney—she replied, mysteriously, “When I moved to China.” Matters fell apart quickly
She appeared on Sean Hannity’s show, perhaps expecting the tender treatment for which Hannity is so synonymous that his last name has become a portmanteau, hannitize , for friendly damage control
Instead he subjected her to an interrogation for which she was predictably unprepared
Indeed, her defense consisted of describing herself as unprepared. “What I feel is I really stepped up to the plate with very little prep time

Given the fact that I’d been on the job less than maybe eight hours and had a briefing book in the morning, I feel like I did my very best, Sean, to deliver for the American people that day.” Sometimes, your best just isn’t good enough
So it is with the whole administration—mired in a losing war and persistent inflation, and flailing about for people to blame for the debacle

title: How Botched Executions Were Handled in Centuries Past
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture

The botched execution of Christa Pike, who survived two injections of what was intended to be a lethal dose of pentobarbital on September 30, is—horrifically—not unique: As my colleague Elizabeth Bruenig wrote , it wasn’t even the first botched execution in Tennessee this year
The fact that officials tried twice to kill her is somewhat more unusual, but not without precedent
Consider the case of Margaret Dickson, a Scottish woman of the early 1700s
Estranged from her husband, Dickson took up work as a domestic in the town of Kelso, where she conceived a child out of wedlock but hid the pregnancy for fear of being shunned
She testified that she’d disposed of the baby after it was stillborn, but the body was found, and she was arrested
Under Scottish law at the time, concealment of a pregnancy was considered evidence of intent to commit infanticide
Dickson was convicted and sentenced to hang in Edinburgh in 1724
Following what was then the practice, Dickson’s execution was public
She was hanged; her body was placed in a coffin and carted away for burial (by some accounts following a tussle with body snatchers who hoped to procure the corpse for dissection by medical students)
Along the way, the burial party stopped for a beer, at which point noise was heard from inside the coffin
The lid was pried off, and Dickson was found alive, though confused
Dickson’s survival became an object of fascination and Dickson herself a sort of folk hero, the historian Mikki Brock , the author of a forthcoming book about Dickson, told me
Authorities in Edinburgh initially sought to rehang her, but they were never able to marshal enough support to do so
Dickson, who came to be nicknamed “Half-Hangit Maggie” (that is, half-hanged ), lived into the 1750s
Or take Joseph Samuel, a criminal who was sent from England to a penal colony in Australia
Once there, he was implicated in the murder of a police officer investigating a robbery
Samuel was convicted and sentenced to hang in September 1803, also publicly
On the first try, the rope around Samuel’s neck snapped
By then, the crowd was growing restive; a hasty third attempt also ended with a broken rope

Observers at the scene concluded that the mishaps were a sign from God that Samuel should not be killed, and the governor apparently concurred, commuting Samuel’s sentence to life imprisonment. (Three years later, Samuel disappeared at sea during an escape attempt with other convicts and was presumed drowned; perhaps God’s view was not as clear as it seemed at the gallows.) A third celebrated case was that of John “Babbacombe” Lee, who was convicted of the 1884 murder of his employer and sentenced to die. (By that point, executions in Britain had moved out of the public and into prison yards.) Just like Samuel, Lee was spared by malfunctioning equipment: A trapdoor under the gallows, meant to release the condemned and snap his neck, had been tested, yet it failed three times to open

Lee’s sentence was commuted to life by the British home secretary, Sir William Harcourt, who said, “It would shock the feelings of anyone if a man had twice to pay the pangs of imminent death.” Lee was eventually paroled in 1907
Now infamous as “the man they couldn’t hang,” he wrote an autobiography and was the subject of a 1912 silent film, but he then faded from the historical record
He appears to have died in the 1940s, perhaps in Milwaukee
When I first heard the stories of Half-Hangit Maggie and Babbacombe Lee as a child, I knew they were historical, but they seemed to belong more to the realm of myth or fairy tale
Hangings, mysterious mechanical failures, assertions of divine intervention—all of these seemed like things out of fiction
It was easy to chuckle at quaint details, such as the apocryphal tale that Dickson was required to remarry her husband because she’d been declared dead
And though I’d read about the beheadings of Charles I and Louis XVI, the specter of public execution felt distant enough from modern civilization to be faintly unreal
Now all of these things seem much less remote
Until President Trump reversed course yesterday, the Defense Department planned to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, who massacred comrades at Fort Hood in 2009
Pike’s fate is up in the air after her twice-failed execution
Pike, who was convicted of a brutal murder in 1995, has returned from a hospital to prison
The state official who oversaw capital punishment has resigned, and the governor has temporarily paused all executions in Tennessee
Her lawyers have requested that her sentence be commuted to life in prison
The doctor and ethicist Lydia Dugdale writes in The Dispatch that U.S. history offers a grim precedent
In 1946, a 16-year-old boy confessed to killing his employer and was sentenced to die via electrocution
A first attempt failed, and his lawyers sought to block a second
The Supreme Court ruled against them, and he was killed that year

But Dugdale argues that this precedent should not apply here. “From Pike’s markedly swollen and chemically burned arms, to her profound cognitive impairment (the severity of which remains unknown), the state has already inflicted a cruel and unusual punishment on Christa,” she writes

Setting aside the law, “as a matter of sheer ethics, if the state has vowed not to punish prisoners cruelly but has inadvertently done so, the state ought not attempt the same method of execution again.” (In this year’s other botched Tennessee case, Tony Carruthers’s failed execution left him partially paralyzed

title: The Real Selling Point of Romantasy
excerpt: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books
body: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books
Romantasy—the category of fiction in which the supernaturally gifted soar on the wings of love, and also sometimes of dragons—is incredibly successful
Maas, has sold about 75 million copies of her novels, my colleague Honor Jones reported in a recent Atlantic essay
The appeal of the genre, Jones found, isn’t just chiseled abs, smoldering gazes, and faerie frippery

Yes, there are hyper-athletic magical trysts, but “far more significant are feelings and friendships between the heroes: enchanted beings with relatable self-esteem issues who don’t just seek and fight but also yearn and banter as they face down enemies,” Jones writes
Readers stay for engaging and emotionally effective stories featuring characters they love
First, here are four new stories from The Atlantic ’s Books section: Good villains are hard to come by
The journalist and the manipulator Immigration is a poorly oiled machine

The man who wanted to understand every aspect of Jewish life Romantasy fans generally know that books like those in Maas’s mega-best-selling A Court of Thorns and Roses series—popularly known by the acronym ACOTAR —aren’t going to win the Pulitzer Prize

And they know that fantasy isn’t real life. “But if they’re snowed in—­or trapped by a pandemic, or up with a nursing newborn, or stuck in any of the ways humans tend to get stuck—­it can help to imagine” the possibility of magic, Jones writes
This reading experience doesn’t require the emotional tumult of picturing oneself in, say, Oliver Twist’s tiny 19th-century orphan shoes—or, more challenging, Fagin’s villainous boots

Instead, ACOTAR and its ilk make imagining easy: You may not know what it’s like to kiss a shape-shifter, but it’s exciting—seductive, even—to picture giving in to an attraction tinged with intrigue and mystery
And doing so is not necessarily less fulfilling than reading literary fare, because practicing this kind of creativity is good for us
It makes life’s hardships more bearable, as Jones indicates, and it also makes reality more interesting
If all we did was describe the mundane to one another, it would be difficult for any of us to have the kind of life worth writing stories about

Jones notes that plenty of people in the literary world “lament that the only books that sell now are faerie or dragon or elfpunk porn.” But a better approach would be to learn from romantasy’s success: We sometimes need a reminder that reading can simply be entertaining

And if entertainment comes from imagining what it might be like to have a hunky elf-king hanging around, well, where’s the harm in that? Illustration by Natalie Shields Those Books of Smut and Wonder By Honor Jones How Sarah J
Maas became the queen of romantasy Read the full article

What to Read The Fox Wife , by Yangsze Choo Choo’s novel, set in Manchuria in 1908, blends folklore and classic detective fiction, and adds a dash of fantasy—half of its characters are shape-shifting spirits who transform from foxes to humans and back again
These creatures are as clever and crafty as you might expect, and the narrative twists keep the reader in a state of high alert
What starts as a police procedural about the death of a high-class courtesan soon blossoms into a fantastical quest to break curses, rekindle lost love, and catch a murderer
Although it’s not overly long, the book has a mythic feeling, moving through time and space like an epic poem
Choo seamlessly combines narrative momentum and lush world-building, so the reader discovers the setting and uncovers the mystery alongside the novel’s endearing detective. — M

I once walked past her in a Chicago O’Hare bathroom in 2016, shortly after Donald Trump had won his first presidential election, and was momentarily stopped in my tracks by both her nuclear-grade charisma and her pixie cut

title: What Newsrooms Should Know Before They Take Money From OpenAI
excerpt: As a newsroom executive, I have long tried to resist appeals to vet donors to nonprofit journalism for their politics or even the savoriness of their business p
body: As a newsroom executive, I have long tried to resist appeals to vet donors to nonprofit journalism for their politics or even the savoriness of their business practices

When you do that, you raise questions about whether you could fairly cover any potential donors on your banned list, and you also run the risk of offering some sort of implicit endorsement to the rest
Both of those perceptions are antithetical to the independent stance that good journalism requires
To take one notorious example, we never received a check from the Koch family’s interests when I was running the business side of ProPublica, but I would have been happy to take it if we had
Nor am I one of those people who think that it makes sense to refuse corporate contributions
Almost all major donors derive the money they are offering from a successful corporation
With that said, I want to offer some cautionary thoughts on the largesse from the company that has become the leading corporate supporter of American journalism, OpenAI

In gifts through its People-First AI Fund, and in large grants disbursed through the American Journalism Project and the Lenfest Institute for Journalism (both occasional consulting clients of mine), OpenAI has distributed $25 million in cash to U.S. newsrooms in the past few years, a large multiple of the journalism grants from Microsoft and Google
OpenAI has also made a number of significant one-off gifts, so its total is considerably larger

Anthropic has not yet joined this party. ( The Atlantic has a content-licensing agreement with OpenAI, although it does not receive grant funding from the company.) I know that the money is needed, and I am not questioning the uses to which it is currently being put
I think newsrooms need to be more creative in the use of AI, not less; more innovative; and less afraid of the implications for particular kinds of work that may become outmoded
Here’s what I think the recipients need to bear in mind
The company’s motivation here is not altruistic
OpenAI says that its intent is “to benefit all of humanity,” but we know that some people there and elsewhere worry that it is, in fact, going to end up snuffing out humanity

We also see that, in the face of such warnings, the company races along, its CEO announcing that “the world should accept some bad things happening.” More narrowly, the firm’s spending on supporting news is almost certainly seen internally as a form of marketing and public relations, helping to spur product adoption and perhaps blunt any impulses toward regulation or taxation, both of which seem to be crucially and urgently necessary
The money may be material to us, but it isn’t to them

It should be sobering, for instance, that OpenAI spent roughly the same amount of money trying to intervene in a single Manhattan congressional primary this past spring as it has in newsroom funding over the years through Lenfest. [ Matteo Wong: OpenAI has gone rogue ] Our worldviews are at fundamental variance
The core principles of journalism focus on the search for accuracy with fairness and the discovery of truth
The essence of the business of generative artificial intelligence seems to be the maximization of profit , whether or not other goals are achieved
The spigot could shut off at any time, and likely eventually will
We have been down this road before with tech firms, and need to assume that this funding won’t be sustained, and shouldn’t be part of any plan for sustainability
Facebook was a significant funder of news until it not only wasn’t, but then took steps to choke off the flow of news to its users

Google purported to be especially solicitous of news until, in my view , it detected insufficient gratitude and greater support for regulation (especially in Canada) and largely reversed course. ( The Atlantic has received grant funding in the past from Facebook and Google but no longer accepts such grants to fund its journalism.) Inside the velvet glove is a mailed fist

Journalists should never forget that there is significant evidence that OpenAI has built its enormous machine in small but significant (at least to us) part by appropriating our intellectual property without compensation
That’s a nice way of saying that the company is arguing in court that it has the right to take our lifeblood while laying waste to important parts of our business
This is ultimately a legal question, but one in which the company—and, to be sure, its competitors at Anthropic, Google, Meta, and Microsoft—is our adversary
The stakes in those fights may be existential for newsrooms; they will not be for the platforms

When creating new AI tools or devising new methods or products using AI that are ultimately funded by an AI company, journalists owe it to their readers, listeners, and viewers to let them know about that funding
Don’t limit the disclosure to an intermediary source through which the money passed
Innovation needs to be coupled with accountability

Even as OpenAI and, to a lesser extent, some of its competitors are paying newsrooms for more rapid and clever adoption of their products and services, it’s very important that anyone taking this funding also invest commensurately in increased accountability for these behemoths and the havoc they are wreaking in some local communities, many funding streams, and, moving forward, job markets
I do have faith in the ability of editors and publishers to maintain editorial independence from funders; I have seen it in action many times
But the larger the portions of food on offer, the greater the temptation not to bite the hand offering it

We need to help one another to resist this, including by pointing out compromises among colleagues if and when we see them. [ Jessica Lessin: Media companies are making a huge mistake with AI ] One important caveat: I am far less concerned about the explosion almost certainly ahead in individual philanthropy derived from AI than I am about the direct provision of corporate funds
There may be issues with some individuals, of course
But the multiplicity of likely funders will help, as will their varying motivations
The truth is that corporate philanthropy has always been something of an oxymoron
The duty of corporations is to their shareholders, and specifically to the maximizing of shareholder value
Journalists can take some comfort that, in companies with more enlightened management, this objective is sought over the long run, which may more closely align with societal interests
Managers with more limited vision, as well as those so enamored of their own capabilities as to conflate society’s objectives with their own, present a less happy case

title: Will the New ‘Grand Theft Auto’ Be a Weapon in the Culture Wars?
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In the newest Grand Theft Auto installment—13 years and estimated billions of dollars in the making—people in
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In the newest Grand Theft Auto installment—13 years and estimated billions of dollars in the making—people in a fictionalized version of Florida can exercise, drink smoothies, pet their dog, go to the club, and so much more
The main characters are in a relationship, and players will have to tend to that too

Galaxy Brain host Charlie Warzel talks with the gaming journalist Chris Plante about why the details of this game matter, the controversies it may unleash, the weirdest things he’s seen happen in the game, and what Grand Theft Auto tells us about America in 2026

The following is a transcript of the episode: Charlie Warzel: Is there a possibility that you can’t make a game for everyone in 2026? Chris Plante: I think it’s like saying the NFL season might not land this year because people are worried about CTE, or people are worried about people kneeling in the end zone
Like there’s always those things that people say, like: This is it; this is the year that I don’t watch it
And then it’s the biggest season ever for the NFL

Charlie Warzel: I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain , a show where, today, we’re gonna be talking about what is poised to be the biggest, most expensive, and arguably most controversial piece of culture and entertainment in recent memory
It is an event that is 13 years in the making
Yes, we’re talking about Grand Theft Auto VI
Now, you might not be a video-game person, but chances are you know about Grand Theft Auto

And maybe that’s because you’ve played some version since 2001, when Rockstar, the studio that makes the franchise, released GTA 3 , which was the first version of the game to turn what was a small-budget carjacking game into a cinematic, 3-D, open-world experience

Or maybe you’ve sat on the couch and you’ve watched with either glee or horror as somebody else—your partner, your child, your friend—went on a brutal crime spree, getting chased around the city by fleets of police cars and helicopters
Or maybe you know the game through its controversies

To list a few: There’s been outrage over cop killing; the way that the game has depicted sex workers; the fact that sex workers are in the game at all; depictions of torture; celebrities claiming their likenesses have been used; and, of course, the concerns that the game could lead to real-world violence
But no matter what your experience, Grand Theft Auto is something else, too
For 25 years now, the franchise has been more than a video game
It is one of the most ambitious works of digital art and storytelling that we have
The series has inspired copycats, but it’s also expanded the bounds of what is possible in the gaming format
Each iteration has not only expanded the length of the game, but the size of the world and the scope of the story
Rockstar’s attention to detail in the game—stuff like, after being discharged from the hospital, characters will have cuts and bruises
The series actually seems locked in its own cycle of one-upsmanship, which has moved beyond a video game and into something that feels like its own metaverse
This game, which will take place in a fictional version of Florida, will supposedly allow people to play in a vast portion of the state, all the way from the quays up into the swamps
Now the GTA phenomenon is also borne out in the economics
GTA 5 , which came out in 2013, is still selling like crazy
And it is, depending on which ranking you’re reading, it’s in the top three best-selling games of all time, next to huge online games like Minecraft or Tetris
GTA 6 , which is slated to come out November 19th, is estimated to have cost Rockstar in the billions of dollars to make, and it will be the most anticipated game of all time
And so my guest today is someone who can put all of this into perspective
Chris Plante is the co-founder of Polygon , the gaming website
He’s the host of The Besties and Post Games , two excellent and different podcasts about video games and gaming

Chris has been writing and covering this industry for 20 years, but what I appreciate about his work is that he has this keen eye for the way that this industry interacts with, but also drives, popular culture

So is the world ready for GTA 6 ? In a world that is almost devoid of monocultural events, can Grand Theft Auto deliver on that promise? Can a series that has satirized America, often pretty savagely, take on [Donald] Trump’s America and Florida without making everyone mad or insane? GTA is now an American institution
But the question remains: Can any institution really survive in 2026? Chris Plante joins me now to talk about all of it
So we’re here because Grand Theft Auto VI is coming out soon
And you know, it feels like there are so many things, serious things, happening in the world right now, such that I think the release of this game is gonna sneak up on people
Which is kind of a ridiculous thing to say about a game that people have been anticipating for about a decade, but like seriously for about like four years
And yet I still think it’s going to sneak up on people
But my working theory is that Grand Theft Auto VI is going to be one of the biggest cultural events of the decade
Am I right? Am I wrong? Am I crazy? Talk to me
Plante: It’s the closest thing we have to a guarantee in popular mainstream media, outside of when Avengers: Endgame came out that first time
But this game will be huge, because the one that came out right before this—you know, over a decade ago—it’s still selling about 5 million copies a quarter

title: This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration
excerpt: More than 5 million people around the world with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) experience atrophy in their retinas
body: More than 5 million people around the world with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) experience atrophy in their retinas
And until now, no treatment could restore their vision
The PRIMA system, which was approved in Europe in July and is awaiting FDA clearance in the US, changes that
It combines a retinal implant with camera-­equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision due to advanced AMD
After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients were able to read, do crosswords, and use their phones

The retina processes light in three layers of cells: Photoreceptors convert light into electricity, bipolar cells process that signal, and ganglion cells transmit the signal to the optic nerve and the brain

BROWN BIRD DESIGN Developed by the California-based Science Corporation, the system takes advantage of the fact that AMD doesn’t damage all retinal circuitry; only photoreceptors—the cells that convert light into an electrical signal—die off

PRIMA’s implant mimics those cells and transmits visual information directly to healthy eye circuitry and on to the brain. “We’re leveraging all of the body’s own natural functions to process and transmit the information,” says Frank Brodie, an ophthalmologist at the University of California, San Francisco, and Science Corp.’s chief medical officer for ophthalmology.  BROWN BIRD DESIGN CAPTURE Glasses outfitted with a miniature front-facing camera capture what someone is seeing in real time
The video feed is roughly five megapixels running at 30 frames per second, which is similar to TV
The raw video is transmitted to a connected processor via a fiber-optic cable
CONVERT A small, handheld processor, which can be set on a table or tucked in a pocket, converts the video feed into infrared light signals that route back to the glasses
The device also includes physical buttons that let the wearer adjust contrast, brightness, and zoom
BROWN BIRD DESIGN DISPLAY A laser projector on the glasses faces the wearer and shines pulses of near-infrared light directly at the eye at 880 nanometers—an invisible wavelength
This signal passes through the pupil and on to the retinal implant in the back of the eye
SEE The implant is made up of 378 pixels, each with an electrode and two photovoltaic cells , which do double duty
They convert the light into a current that healthy bipolar and ganglion cells pass on to the brain
They also act as solar cells to power the chip, eliminating the need for a battery
Update : This story has been updated to clarify the specific cases of AMD the PRIMA system treats
Linda Marsa is a former Los Angeles Times reporter and an author who covers medicine, health, science, and the environment.

title: Love is infrastructure
excerpt: Meet cute Barnabas and Mainspring grew up near at hand, about an hour apart with good traffic, but for a long time they weren’t close
body: Meet cute Barnabas and Mainspring grew up near at hand, about an hour apart with good traffic, but for a long time they weren’t close
They traded glimpses and occasional hellos and then went about their business
Both of them carried on livelier conversations with farther-flung neighbors, who were richer and had more to offer
When Mainspring did interact with Barnabas, it was cringe
Mainspring liked to puff themself up, to strut around like a big deal—an innovator, a titan of industry—but they would turn shy at the worst moments, especially in any intimate conversation

Barnabas, meanwhile, had a dancer’s flair, an artsy, enigmatic glamour, except that when they tried to talk about real life, they’d blurt out hundreds of rapid-fire words—overtalking, overthinking, and generally overwhelming whomever they were trying to impress
So when Barnabas and Mainspring were young, they minded their own business
Until they’d both come into their own, and they saw each other properly
A group of geographers got together every year in a different place to talk about everything they had learned, and they were considering coming to visit either Mainspring or Barnabas
Both of them put on their best faces and tried to coax the geographers into choosing them as host. “Uh, hi-hello,” Mainspring said haltingly to Barnabas, whose full official name was St
Barnabas. “I really think it would be better if those geographers came to my place
I have more space, you see, and … and I am a titan of industry
I can show them practical applications of their research
It just makes more sense.” “Oh, really?” Barnabas laughed, making Mainspring more antsy. “Well, I can give them an elevated, artisanal experience
I have fresh croissants that were just written up in the Times
And I have plenty of space! I have so many friends who are great thinkers and architects
It’ll be lovely.” Barnabas carried on, basically calling Mainspring uncultured
Mainspring had a prickly feeling, like the worst heat dome of midsummer
For their part, Barnabas couldn’t bear the meanness they were inculcating inside themself
This feeling that they were small-time, no-account, a dilettante
They couldn’t stop aiming a flood of nervous words at Mainspring
At last, Mainspring had had enough—with the help of their city council and mayor, they offered the geographers a much-too-lavish deal that Barnabas could never hope to match

Totally worth it to hear Barnabas’s stream of self-aggrandizing nonsense peter out as they realized they’d been defeated. “There,” Mainspring said. “I’m going to show these geographers a time they’ll never forget
Now if you’ll excuse me, I’ve wasted enough energy—I have some sewer maintenance and a lovely parade to deal with

Goodbye.” Mainspring was skilled enough at multitasking that they could have fixed the sewer, ensured the smooth running of the parade, dealt with the geographers, and done a thousand other things all at the same time
Barnabas is such a fool,” Mainspring complained to their friend Turnbull. “They are totally unserious but determined to be taken seriously

It drives me to gridlock.” “I know what you mean,” lamented Turnbull. “We live in a world of posers.” Turnbull lived an hour and 15 minutes from Mainspring but at least two hours’ travel from Barnabas

Turnbull was even richer than Mainspring and had a certain surety of purpose that made Mainspring feel even more like a stammering numpty. “Whatever,” said Mainspring. “It’s over, and now I’ll never worry about St
Like ensuring that every last detail of this geographer meeting goes perfectly.” II
How they came alive Everybody voted all the time
Well, some people voted more than others, but the median resident of the cities of Mainspring and St
Barnabas voted a dozen times a day—though of course some outliers might vote occasionally, or constantly
A lot of the votes were more like complaints, or bug tickets

Like: “The storm drain on my street corner clogs and becomes a lagoon every time it rains.” Or: “The cars go too fast on my block.” Or: “I can’t get to work because the bus is too slow.” But there were also votes along the lines of: “There should be a park here.” And: “This neighborhood is a food desert—we need a grocery store.” And: “The crossing guard by the elementary school is a hero who deserves some recognition and maybe a raise.” Nobody expected that by voting, they were prodding their cities to grow minds of their own; they just had stuff to get off their metaphorical chests
But it transpired that every vote was a building block of thought
Much later, some fancy expert summed up: “Turns out the smallest unit of consciousness is a vote.” Take Sandi, the librarian at the Nine Corners branch in Mainspring
She noticed things all day, like the people using the book drop box as a trash can, or the folks who came in off the street who could use easier access to social services
There were books she knew her patrons wanted, books that undoubtedly sat unwanted on people’s shelves all over the city

But also, Sandi shared things that came to mind—like, hey, what if the library book sale were a block party? What if the shopping district on the West Side were easier to get to from the Longneck neighborhood, where all the warehouses had been converted to housing and hipster coworking spaces, during peak after-work hours? Sandi had opinions about everything from street cleaning to the power grid, because she listened to people all day

title: Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered.
excerpt: Pet longevity is a growing area of research: Companies like Loyal are trialing drugs in over 1,300 dogs to combat aging, metabolic disease, and conditions like
body: Pet longevity is a growing area of research: Companies like Loyal are trialing drugs in over 1,300 dogs to combat aging, metabolic disease, and conditions like arthritis — and there's even a longevity medicine company focused entirely on cats

Cloning offers grieving owners "a way to hold on": For $50,000, US company Viagen Pets will create a genetic twin of your dog or cat — not an exact replica, but close enough that some experts see it as a legitimate response to pet loss

Cryonics promises revival, but delivers almost nothing: A handful of companies will freeze your dead pet indefinitely, banking on future technology to bring them back — even those in the field admit reanimation is currently impossible. " data-chronoton-post-id="1146766" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat
I can conjure the sensation of stroking her while she purred, recall how she used to get stuck in trees (just like in cartoons!), and chuckle about the time she pooed in my baby sister’s cot
What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing
I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset
There was no way to get more time with Peppy, but almost 30 years later, pet owners are being offered an ever-expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions
The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics
But is that a good thing? There’s certainly a market for pet preservation
And a growing number of biotech companies have their sights set on pet longevity
Loyal, a company that is currently working on three potential longevity drugs for dogs, is trialing one designed to improve metabolic health in around 1,300 pet dogs across the US
Others are testing dog drugs that aim to combat both age-related diseases, including conditions like obesity and osteoarthritis , and aging itself
There’s even a company focused on longevity medicines for domesticated cats
But if there had been a drug that might have protected her from diabetes or arthritis, there’s no doubt I would have tried to get my hands on it
That’s about where my enthusiasm for pet life extension ends, though
I’m far less interested in cloning, a relatively new option for people mourning a pet and seeking a replacement
In most cases, this technology involves taking the DNA of a pet, putting it into an egg cell from another animal of the same species, and growing the resulting embryo in a surrogate animal
It worked for Dolly the sheep, who was born the year before Peppy went missing
It has since worked for other mammals, including cattle, horses, and ferrets—and cats and dogs
In the US, a company called Viagen Pets offers to clone cats and dogs for $50,000 a go
This doesn’t result in an exact replica of the animal but a genetic twin
Still, there are lots of reasons why a person might want to clone a pet

On its website, Viagen explicitly offers customers “a way to hold on.” Lori Kogan, a professor of clinical sciences at Colorado State University who has studied human-animal relationships for decades, doesn’t have a problem with the practice
She points out that while we have well-established rituals for coping with the loss of a person—such as funeral services, time off work, and memorial gifts—we don’t really have the same for pets
As a result, pet owners can experience what is sometimes called “disenfranchised grief,” she says
Having their feelings go unrecognized can feel isolating
If cloning a pet brings a person peace, she says, “who are we to judge?” Fair enough
But I can’t help thinking that pet loss in childhood might be different
It’s often the first time a child confronts death
Losing Peppy was a formative experience, and distressing though it was, I like to think it helped prepare me for losses I experienced in adulthood
I wouldn’t want my own children to think that death is not final, and that individuals can be replicated or replaced
Or, for that matter, revived, which is the promise behind pet cryonics
For a fee, a handful of companies offer to cool dead pets to extremely low temperatures and store them for long periods of time—even indefinitely
The idea is that at some point in the future, we’ll have invented incredible technologies that will not only bring your pet back to life but also cure whatever it died of
Alcor , a cryonics facility in Arizona, is currently storing the remains of hundreds of pets as well as people
It even recently announced it had cooled a small marsupial—its first pet sugar glider
With cryonics, the chances of being reunited with your pet are bordering on zero
Even those who work in the field acknowledge that the stored people and animals are unlikely to be reanimated
As things stand, there is no way to really and truly bring any animal “back.” I miss Peppy
But given the chance, would I stick her in a vat of liquid nitrogen? Or get another cat to give birth to a genetically identical animal? No, I would not

title: Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.
excerpt: In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by
body: In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds
The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15
But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented
A study published earlier this year found that four in five teens under 16 made their way onto barred platforms

Teens have successfully explored many tactics for bypassing bans, from using a sibling’s face for ID to drawing fake facial hair.  Some proponents of bans have called for an increased focus on enforcement that blocks these workarounds
But circumvention is a signal, not a nuisance or something to be simply deterred
The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations
Social media bans suppress kids’ access to information, including information that’s essential to their development, identity formation, and socialization, especially during adolescence
Worse, further restriction is likely to backfire
Closing loopholes in age gates could harm kids by pushing them toward less-moderated, higher-risk corners of the web
It also degrades privacy and security for everyone by forcing people to submit sensitive personal information to prove their age
In our work , we’ve found that parents and kids both want smarter, more nuanced policies that protect children, families, and their rights

That can take the form of mandating stronger limits on data collection by companies, or giving families flexible tools to control content and access on their own terms.  Age gates won’t bring about the desired change, nor will they simplify parenting in the digital world
At best, they will only raise thornier questions and postpone the conversation to a child’s 16th birthday
At worst, they’ll leave kids with no guidance as they make their way through the online world

A less safe internet for kids When young people circumvent restrictions, they are often doing what we want developing minds to do and what we celebrate in other contexts: lean into curiosity, problem-solve, and exercise independence
It’s important for kids to do this online, an arena where they often develop social skills and refine their identities
Bans sweep these motivations under the rug, taking a paternalistic approach that doesn’t consider young people’s needs or the realities of what they do online.  It also ignores what some parents want
When we examined social media safety interventions last year, parents told us that they often join their kids in lies that help them gain access to needed but gated services
This isn’t a new phenomenon; research all the way back in 2011 showed that parents taught their children how to evade Facebook age restrictions
Some may say these parents are oblivious to the harms posed by the web or just don’t care
Many simply see offering their children responsible access to social media as a way to help them connect with like-minded peers, find informational content, and learn digital safety skills early on

Many parents believe the benefits outweigh the risks.  When parents don’t help provide access and kids are not able to get into the platforms they desire, they will likely move toward alternative online spaces, often ones with fewer guardrails
Sometimes kids wind up on fairly innocuous, if unconventional , platforms, communicating with each other in Google Docs or podcast comment sections
Other times they move to more dangerous platforms that can leave them vulnerable to abuse and predation

In the aftermath of the Australian social media ban, preliminary research shows that kids’ screen time has not meaningfully decreased but has sometimes been redirected, with some young users going to spaces that are unmonitored and unknown to parents
Just as cities are sketchiest when they are not bustling, the most risky platforms for young people are those with the fewest eyes on the digital street
Outdated, dying, and under-resourced platforms tend to attract both vulnerable youth and those who prey on them
A less safe internet for all Age gates come with dangers of their own
Some platforms automatically track users’ online activities to confirm their age

In doing so, they profile users—collecting and analyzing their data to make inferences about them, which can increase the risk that data will be misused or leaked.  Companies may also ask for personal documents like driver’s licenses to verify age, which can lead to mishandling of sensitive documents or even identity theft

Data breaches happen: Last year, for example, Discord reported that one of its third-party services, 5CA, which is used to confirm age, had been compromised, exposing at least 70,000 images of users’ government IDs

It can take little effort to find ways to use that kind of information for malicious purposes by, say, connecting driver’s licenses to specific accounts and private online activity, which could reveal anything from users’ political opinions to their sexual preferences.  Efforts to make it harder for kids to get around age gates have also led policymakers to clamp down on kids’ access to VPNs

State age verification bills in Michigan and Utah have tried to interfere with the privacy protections offered by these tools (the Utah bill is now blocked by a federal court ), and Australia’s eSafety Commissioner is nudging social media platforms to detect and block their use
But requiring adult users to prove their age to gain access to a VPN fundamentally defeats the purpose of that privacy-focused technology
It can put many users, particularly journalists and human rights defenders working on sensitive issues, in danger of government surveillance and even retaliation

What could work instead? Rather than attempting to block young people from online services that allow them to access information and engage in age-essential communication, policymakers should focus on the incentives that drive companies to engage in behavior that creates risks for kids in the first place.  For example, platforms should decrease what experts call unhealthy engagement or addictive activity by limiting the collection and use of data that companies use to target content and features to all users, including children
Nearly all parents and teens we spoke with want policymakers to impose such restrictions, knowing full well that the companies’ use of data is at the core of features such as targeted advertisements
Both teens and parents are also frustrated by features designed to keep us all online for longer than we want
Another approach would be to expand the availability of user-controlled tools so that families have easy, flexible, and user-friendly ways to limit access to what is undesirable

title: Young voters fear mass shootings like the one in Oregon, but that fear divides them on gun control
url:
<title>Young voters fear mass shootings like the one in Oregon, but that fear divides them on gun control</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766762/original/file-20261016-50-fzfgcm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3977%2C2652&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">People leave a family meeting area following a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School on Oct. 15, 2026, in Bend, Ore.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Oregon%20School%20Shooting/83d35196352f423ca913c945621f97bc/photo">AP Photo/Joe Kline</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>A gunman shot and killed three children and a teacher at a <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/16/us/live-news/bend-oregon-school-shooting">school in Bend, Oregon</a>, on Oct. 15, 2026, the <a href="https://www.cnn.com/us/school-shootings-fast-facts-dg">52nd school shooting this year</a>, according to CNN. The children’s ages were 5, 8 and 11; a 7-year-old and another teacher were taken to the hospital with critical injuries. The 16-year-old shooting suspect was shot and killed by a bystander.</p>

<p>Though Oregon has <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/us/oregon-gun-control-laws.html">stricter gun laws than most states</a>, some of those laws, such as a measure requiring tougher background checks and requiring a person to have a permit in order to buy a gun, are stalled in court.</p>

<p>The Bend shooting – the latest in a long line of modern school shootings dating back to <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/law/stockton-massacre/">the late 1980s</a> – comes just weeks before the midterm elections, in which voters will choose members of Congress and state lawmakers who can shape gun laws. </p>

<p>Nearly <a href="https://circle.tufts.edu/latest-research/49-million-young-people-will-be-eligible-vote-2026-midterms">50 million Americans</a> ages 18 to 29 are eligible to vote in the upcoming midterm elections, and <a href="https://now.tufts.edu/2026/09/22/young-voters-flex-their-power">about 60% say they plan to</a>. If they follow through, it would break midterm turnout records for voters under 30.</p>

<p><a href="https://now.tufts.edu/2026/09/22/young-voters-flex-their-power">Gun control</a> is an issue these young voters care about more than the public at large does, and it’s easy to understand why: In their lifetime, mass shootings have been <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.13148">a recurring part of American life</a>. </p>

<p>Directly experiencing a mass shooting is rare, yet some young people have survived two before turning 25. When a gunman opened fire at Brown University in December 2025, <a href="https://www.thecut.com/article/brown-university-shooting-parkland-survivor.html">at least two students</a> on campus had already experienced a school shooting before they got to college. The same thing happened in April 2025, when students who lived through <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2018/02/15/us/florida-shooting-victims-school">the 2018 Parkland, Florida, shooting</a> at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School found themselves caught in another shooting at <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2025/04/19/us/florida-state-university-shooting-what-we-know">Florida State University</a>. As <a href="https://www.local10.com/news/local/2025/04/17/parkland-school-massacre-survivor-was-at-fsu-during-fatal-shooting/">one of them</a> put it: “This is America.”</p>

<p>Researchers have called <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.13148">today’s young adults</a> the “massacre generation.” They’re the first group to grow up entirely in the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2019/apr/19/columbine-parkland-how-mass-shootings-changed-us-schools">post-9/11, post-Columbine High School shooting era</a>, with routine <a href="https://nces.ed.gov/fastfacts/display.asp?id=954">lockdown drills</a>, heightened <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2022/07/06/the-school-security-industry-was-valued-at-3point1-billion-in-2021.html">security in schools</a> and nonstop <a href="https://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/news/media-exposure-mass-violence-can-fuel-cycle-distress-study-shows">media coverage of mass violence</a>.</p>

<p>As criminologists who study the impacts of <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=cbfYVuoAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">victimization and gun violence</a> among <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=X52GgbIAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">young people</a>, we wanted to know how growing up with the threat of mass shootings has shaped young adults’ views on gun legislation. In <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.70087">a recent study</a>, we surveyed nearly 1,700 young adults, ages 18 to 29, across the country to find out. We found that fear of mass shootings pulls this generation apart along political and gender lines: It pushes some toward wanting stricter gun laws and others in the opposite direction.</p>

<h2>A debate that repeats after every shooting</h2>

<p>Mass shootings account for <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/04/28/what-the-data-says-about-gun-deaths-in-the-us/">about 1% of gun deaths</a> in the U.S. Still, they profoundly shape how safe millions of Americans feel. In a 2019 <a href="https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/stress/2019/stress-america-2019.pdf">survey by the American Psychological Association</a>, nearly 80% of Americans said the possibility of a mass shooting stressed them out, and a third said they <a href="https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2019/08/fear-mass-shooting">avoided certain places because of it</a>. The fear has become so common that clinicians now have <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/07481187.2023.2214889">screening tools</a> to assess and treat people with anxiety over mass violence.</p>

<p>Young adults have also grown up watching the same <a href="https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article313732975.html">heated gun debates</a> play out after every tragedy. <a href="https://www.everytown.org/issues/mass-shootings/">Gun control advocates</a> call for <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.12857">stricter firearm restrictions</a> to prevent <a href="https://www.wired.com/story/the-looser-a-states-gun-laws-the-more-mass-shootings-it-has/">the next mass shooting</a>, whereas <a href="https://tpusa.com/live/mass-shootings-are-not-a-reason-for-gun-control/">gun rights advocates</a> push back with the “good guy with a gun” argument, a phrase <a href="https://www.npr.org/2012/12/21/167824766/nra-only-thing-that-stops-a-bad-guy-with-a-gun-is-a-good-guy-with-a-gun">made popular by the National Rifle Association</a>. Supporters of the latter view say more armed citizens are needed to stop active shooters, so more people should be able to buy and carry guns with fewer restrictions, such as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.70087">carrying in public without a permit or on college campuses</a>. </p>

<p>Researchers have known for a long time that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/00027162231164865">more guns don’t necessarily mean less violence</a>. A <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/07418825.2020.1789693">2021 study</a> found that mass shootings were more common in states with higher rates of gun ownership, and gun homicides were more common in states with looser concealed carry laws. Yet even after <a href="https://www.researchgate.net/publication/390806181_NIJ_Final_Report_A_Comprehensive_Assessment_of_Deadly_Mass_Shootings_1980-2018">decades of mass shootings</a>, federal gun policy has <a href="https://www.bu.edu/articles/2022/the-long-failed-history-of-gun-control-legislation/">barely budged</a>. Even where individual states and local governments have passed assault weapons bans, including <a href="https://portal.ct.gov/ag/press-releases/2026-press-releases/attorney-general-statement-on-scotus-certification-in-challenge-to-connecticut-assault-weapon-ban">Connecticut</a> and <a href="https://www.jurist.org/news/2026/07/us-supreme-court-agrees-to-hear-challenges-to-assault-weapons-bans/">Cook County, Illinois</a>, they’ve faced <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-the-assault-weapons-debate-is-a-culture-debate-291639">Second Amendment challenges that are now before the Supreme Court</a>.</p>

<p>Young people have become some of the <a href="https://time.com/7304031/march-for-our-lives-pam-bondi-shootings-jaclyn-corin/">loudest voices in this debate</a>, most notably through <a href="https://marchforourlives.org/">March for Our Lives</a> – an organization started by Parkland survivors that focuses on ending gun violence – and <a href="https://www.texastribune.org/2018/06/28/texas-gun-control-high-school-student-activists-santa-fe-mass-shooting/">other youth-led groups</a> across the country. And because pro-gun views tend to be more common among <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/07/24/key-facts-about-americans-and-guns/">older Americans</a>, many political observers assume <a href="https://iop.harvard.edu/press-releases/harvard-iop-youth-poll-finds-stricter-gun-laws-ban-assault-weapons-favored-two">stricter gun laws will follow</a> as young people <a href="https://now.tufts.edu/2026/09/22/young-voters-flex-their-power">gain voting power</a>.</p>

<p>This fall, voters in a few states will weigh in on gun policy directly.</p>

<p>In Massachusetts, voters will decide whether to <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_9,_Firearm_Regulations_Referendum_(2026)">keep or repeal a 2024 law</a> that, among other things, requires gun owners to register their firearms with the state, expands safety training for people applying for a gun license and broadens the state’s ban on assault-style weapons. In Arkansas, they’ll decide whether to <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Arkansas_Issue_2,_Right_to_Keep_and_Bear_Arms_Amendment_(2026)">change the state constitution</a> to more strongly protect gun rights, including the right to own ammunition and gun parts. If young adults turn out in record numbers, their views could help determine outcomes like these.</p>

<h2>Young adults are split</h2>

<p>So where do young adults stand? We’ve found that a shared fear of mass shootings does not necessarily lead to shared views on guns. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.70087">Our survey asked</a> young adults to rate on a scale from 1 to 3 – from “not at all” to “a lot” – how much they fear that they or someone they love will become a victim of a mass shooting. More than 60% reported moderate or high levels of fear, including about 17% who fell in the high-fear range.</p>

<p>In general, about two-thirds of young adults said people should need a permit to carry a gun in public and that guns shouldn’t be allowed on college campuses. About 6 in 10 disagreed that owning more guns makes people safer, and a similar share disagreed that gun control laws are unconstitutional.</p>

<p>We found that young adults who worried more about mass shootings tended to be more supportive of gun control. But this pattern didn’t hold for young men, Republicans or those who were politically conservative. For these groups, the opposite was true: The more they feared mass shootings, the less they supported gun restrictions. Young adults are divided on gun control, and those divisions are sharpest when fear runs high. </p>

<p>In the coming years, the massacre generation is on track to become part of the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12340">largest voting bloc in the country</a>. Most young adults share a fear of mass shootings, but they disagree on what to do about them. And with each new mass shooting, that divide may only deepen.</p>

<title>Remote work made these colleagues more open with each other, not less</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765671/original/file-20261012-60-gamskh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7360%2C4906&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Many employees see having the freedom to work from home as a benefit.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/black-entrepreneur-wearing-headphones-on-video-royalty-free-image/1369954837?adppopup=true">DigitalVision/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>If you need to participate in video meetings for work, you’ve probably experienced more than one disruption, whether it’s kids darting around or home renovation noise.</p>

<p>Meetings that use Zoom and similar software are a fixture of remote work, which <a href="https://www.census.gov/library/publications/2023/acs/acs-52.html">surged during the COVID-19 pandemic</a> and remains prevalent. As of August 2026, <a href="https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cpseea42.htm">36% of American workers</a> in management, professional and related occupations did at least some of their work from home, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.</p>

<p>I’m a management scholar who studies <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=3I0eCFcAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">how, when and where people work</a>. Before the pandemic began, I was studying a professional services company. That made it possible for me to follow how its staff transitioned from primarily working in person to mostly remote through 2024, which gave me more insight into how remote work has changed people’s lives.</p>

<p>The study included 275 interviews and about 330 hours of observation. Most people in the groups I followed ended up working from home four or five days a week, joining meetings by video. What I found was the opposite of what I expected.</p>



<h2>Learning more about colleagues</h2>

<p>Rather than pulling colleagues apart, remote work brought them closer and made them more willing to be open with one another. The findings were peer-reviewed and will be <a href="https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2024.19818">published in an upcoming issue</a> of the management journal Organization Science.</p>

<p>Before the shift to remote work, I assumed – consistent with the predictions made by many prominent <a href="https://hbr.org/2021/04/what-psychological-safety-looks-like-in-a-hybrid-workplace">researchers of workplace relationships</a> – that moving people out of the office would break down social connections. But I was wrong.</p>

<p>In the office, before the shift to remote work, I found that people primarily viewed one another as work colleagues rather than whole people. Reflecting this relationship, workers sometimes said they felt uncomfortable sharing with one another aspects of their lives that might limit their ability to do work.</p>

<p>For example, one worker I interviewed, Patrick, was afraid to tell his colleagues he could not work late one night because he was helping his mom. All the names I’m mentioning are pseudonyms to protect the privacy of the people involved and their employer.</p>

<p>“Even though you didn’t sleep last night, you’re expected to show up and smile and be fine,” said Tamara, an exhausted parent with two young children, when she was still commuting regularly to the office.</p>

<p>Surprisingly, people told me that they learned a lot more about one another once they began to work remotely instead of being together in an office. During my research, I heard about children yelling in the background and pets wandering in front of cameras. A spouse arriving home from work stopped to say hello on screen. </p>

<p>In team chat channels, people posted photos of their children, their animals and the meals they had cooked.</p>

<p>“Everyone has noises in the background, or they have something going on or whatever, and so we get to know each other quicker and on a deeper level than we would otherwise,” Tamara told me. In some cases, this increased sense of closeness happened to people who had known each other for years prior to switching to remote work.  </p>

          </figure>

<h2>Growing psychological safety</h2>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-031413-091305">Psychological safety</a> is the sense that you can take an interpersonal risk at work, such as admitting a mistake, asking for help or raising a problem, without being judged negatively.</p>

<p>Decades of management research tie psychological safety to important outcomes for both workers and organizations, including <a href="https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-120920-055217">learning, creativity and speaking up</a>.</p>

<p>Over time, working remotely seemed to improve psychological safety for many of these co-workers.</p>

<p>People became “less afraid to talk about the interface of their personal and professional lives,” Leah said. Before, she added, no one would have volunteered that a breakup was affecting them and that they needed a day off to decompress.</p>

<p>After the company went remote, people told me they felt more comfortable sharing their own challenges as they tried to juggle their work and the challenges they faced in their personal lives.</p>

<h2>Supporting work and nonwork activities</h2>

<p>And as people started sharing these problems with their co-workers, they also told me they felt as if they could then better support one another.</p>

<p>When one worker’s father fell ill, his colleague, Brooke, took over the tasks the two had planned to do together. </p>

<p>“I’m just going to take this over for you right now,” Brooke told him. “And then, whenever you can, come back and swoop in.”</p>

<p>The colleague was able to dedicate time to caring for his father. And importantly, because help circulated this way, Brooke said, a task no longer “stopped dead in the water” when one person could not get to it.</p>

<p>This deeper collaboration did not seem to come at the expense of getting tasks completed. As an employee I’m calling Charles explained, having co-workers sharing details about their personal lives has “helped us to work more effectively in a lot of ways.”</p>

<p>Crucially, these improvements were experienced by people with many different living arrangements – young and old, those with and without kids or partners, men and women. And these benefits were positively reinforcing. For instance, sharing more meant learning more about others, which further reinforced psychological safety.</p>

<p>My findings suggest that remote work can be a benefit that employers and employees may overlook. Rather than treating time out of the office as a cost to social connection among employees, they might treat it as a way to grow personally and get to know co-workers better.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291728/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Belonging and belief: Why evangelical churches draw many migrants in the US</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766547/original/file-20261015-50-c4nx4m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1024%2C682&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">People pray during a service in a storefront church in the Little Havana neighborhood of Miami, Fla.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/louis-enrique-originally-from-nicaragua-prays-during-a-news-photo/76043617?phrase=evangelical%20church%20immigrant%20u.s.&amp;adppopup=true">Joe Raedle/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>In October 2024, right before the presidential election, I had coffee with Kim, a Congolese asylum-seeker living in southern Maine. Our conversation quickly turned to politics, and I cautiously asked about her views, although she could not vote.</p>

<p>During his campaign, Donald Trump <a href="https://www.npr.org/2024/10/30/nx-s1-5170339/trumps-mass-deportation-plan-of-undocumented-migrants-offers-few-specifics">had vowed mass deportations</a>, and I assumed immigration policies would be among her top priorities. </p>

<p>But instead, she quickly turned to matters of faith, invoking her strongly held beliefs. Kim – a pseudonym, like all names used in this article – was an evangelical Christian whose life revolved around her church: a nondenominational congregation led by other Congolese migrants. </p>

<p>“Democrats are not people of God,” she declared. People in her community were “traditional,” she added, and generally wanted politicians who were, too. Congolese Christians, she said, usually believed marriage should only occur between a man and a woman, that sex and gender are chosen by God, and that life is sacred from conception.</p>

<p>Her pronouncement underscores an important but often overlooked reality. Popular commentary in the U.S. often portrays evangelicals as one homogeneous, overwhelmingly white group. In reality, they are diverse, from political views and geography to race: <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/02/26/age-race-education-and-other-demographic-traits-of-us-religious-groups/">3 in 10 U.S. evangelicals are not</a> white.</p>

<p>And <a href="https://www.christianitytoday.com/2024/02/evangelical-immigration-reform-lifeway-safety-threat-econom/">a growing percentage</a> are migrants – a term I use for people who have come to the U.S., regardless of their legal status.</p>

<h2>Belonging and belief</h2>

<p>Overall, 12% of evangelicals in the U.S. were born outside the country, <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/02/26/age-race-education-and-other-demographic-traits-of-us-religious-groups/#immigration-and-region-of-birth">according to a 2024 study</a> conducted by the Pew Research Center. Another 7% have at least one parent born outside the country. These figures are likely underestimates, since undocumented migrants generally avoid surveys for fear of deportation.</p>

<p>As an <a href="https://www.johannarichlin.com/">anthropologist of religion</a>, I’ve studied the growing number of migrants drawn to evangelical faith – and learned how significantly faith shapes their lives in the United States. In turn, these migrants are <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/rowman--littlefield-handbook-of-contemporary-christianity-in-the-united-states-9781538196434/">shaping America’s religious landscape</a>. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766286/original/file-20261014-60-wqj0b9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A small crowd of people stand and raise their arms in prayer as they look downward." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766286/original/file-20261014-60-wqj0b9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766286/original/file-20261014-60-wqj0b9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766286/original/file-20261014-60-wqj0b9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766286/original/file-20261014-60-wqj0b9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766286/original/file-20261014-60-wqj0b9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766286/original/file-20261014-60-wqj0b9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766286/original/file-20261014-60-wqj0b9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/keabeh-goyah-whose-son-is-a-doctor-in-liberia-prays-with-news-photo/456691916?phrase=african%20immigrants%20church%20u.s.&amp;adppopup=true">Joe Raedle/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
