<p>While writing my 2022 book, “<a href="https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691194981/in-the-hands-of-god?srsltid=AfmBOooJMOdCYZBsIP6VCmLVMnZ1SEBZA7uAl2xB81__agiw2ZDFkihU">In the Hands of God</a>,” I spent over a year attending evangelical churches around Washington, D.C., that catered to Brazilian migrants. I interviewed about 80 churchgoers and surveyed dozens more. </p>

<p>Congregants described how belief and belonging helped them overcome challenges such as loneliness, “feeling stuck” due to their legal precariousness and being exploited at work. I heard stories of employers holding migrants’ passports hostage, or refusing to pay construction workers seriously injured on the job.</p>

<p>Migrants often told me that their churches’ close-knit communities, and evangelical Christianity’s emphasis on fostering an intimate relationship with God, <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/26854758">gave them a sense of empowerment</a>. Through prayer, worship, Bible study and fasting, they tried to discern and implement God’s plan for their lives. </p>

<p>The three congregations that I attended offered multiple prayer, study and worship opportunities for migrants throughout the week, both at church and at congregants’ homes. Many pastors were migrants themselves and shared from the pulpit their stories of overcoming adversity. </p>

<p>Gláucia, an undocumented migrant from Brazil, described leaving herself “in the hands of God” as she faced uncertainty about her future. </p>

<p>“I love living here,” she explained. “But if God wants me to leave, I’m under God’s will. Wherever God directs me, I will go. Therefore, I don’t get worried, because we can’t become worried about what comes tomorrow. Because tomorrow belongs to God.</p>

<p>"The most I can do,” she added, “which I always try to do, is pray to God to give direction” to political leaders. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766289/original/file-20261014-50-e10f0l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C53%2C1024%2C576&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Several men bow their heads in prayer as they stand behind blue chairs." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766289/original/file-20261014-50-e10f0l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C53%2C1024%2C576&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766289/original/file-20261014-50-e10f0l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766289/original/file-20261014-50-e10f0l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766289/original/file-20261014-50-e10f0l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766289/original/file-20261014-50-e10f0l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766289/original/file-20261014-50-e10f0l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766289/original/file-20261014-50-e10f0l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Growing communities</h2>

<p>Some people I met identified as evangelical before coming to the U.S., but a significant number were converts. Even among people who had attended evangelical churches in Brazil, many insisted that they truly “met Jesus” in the United States and reflected that their faith back home had been “lukewarm.”</p>

<p>Angela, an undocumented migrant, knew many evangelicals in Brazil. It wasn’t until arriving in the U.S., though, that she converted from Catholicism. She told me, “When you are here, without your family, without any friends, you feel alone, and look for something to hold on to,” she told me. </p>

<p>According to large-scale surveys, <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2013/05/17/the-religious-affiliation-of-us-immigrants/">most immigrants in the U.S. are Christian</a>, and <a href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3629734/">the majority of Christian migrants are Catholic</a>.</p>

<p>Over the past several decades, however, a growing percentage of people in Latin America, long a Catholic stronghold, <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2014/11/13/religion-in-latin-america/">have been embracing evangelical churches</a>. That has influenced the religious makeup of migrants to the United States. Others convert to evangelical Christianity <a href="https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691194981/in-the-hands-of-god?srsltid=AU7gw4VwLjQ6Py74sgZV5QzvMGf1gY-dNFjzbKwU3O2dQ6RbECgptcja">once they arrive</a>, as my research highlights.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766283/original/file-20261014-50-4pbc5w.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="About half a dozen people, some closing their eyes in prayer, sit in church pews." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766283/original/file-20261014-50-4pbc5w.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766283/original/file-20261014-50-4pbc5w.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=900&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766283/original/file-20261014-50-4pbc5w.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=900&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766283/original/file-20261014-50-4pbc5w.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=900&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766283/original/file-20261014-50-4pbc5w.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1130&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766283/original/file-20261014-50-4pbc5w.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1130&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766283/original/file-20261014-50-4pbc5w.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1130&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">People attend Sunday services at the Church of Grace to Fujianese in New York in 2010.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/throngs-of-fujianese-people-file-through-a-doorway-under-news-photo/2175809015?phrase=immigrants%20church&amp;adppopup=true">Najlah Feanny/Corbis via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Most of the migrants I met reported intense psychological pain as they endured  family separation, workplace exploitation and legal uncertainty, which prompted them to search for meaning and comfort in religious spaces. Migrant evangelical churches, they found, <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/26854758">spoke directly to their distress</a>. Their style of worship and theological teachings provided concrete tools, including practices such as prayer, fasting and sharing personal testimony, that relieved migrants’ suffering.</p>

<p>Research suggests it is also common for migrants from other parts of the world, <a href="https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691164663/getting-saved-in-america">including Taiwan</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/3711910">and China</a>, to turn to evangelical, charismatic and Pentecostal churches to address difficulties <a href="https://www.rutgersuniversitypress.org/a-place-to-be/9780813544939">they confront in the United States</a>.</p>

<h2>Changing face of Christianity</h2>

<p>Evangelical churches play a major role in these migrants’ experiences of the U.S. In turn, these migrants are playing a significant role in American Christianity, as I explain in “<a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/rowman--littlefield-handbook-of-contemporary-christianity-in-the-united-states-9781538196434/">The Handbook of Contemporary Christianity in the United States</a>.”  </p>

<p>Over the past few decades, Americans have become <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/02/26/decline-of-christianity-in-the-us-has-slowed-may-have-leveled-off/#trends-in-the-religiousness-of-christians">less Christian and less religious</a>. In 2007, 78% of Americans called themselves Christians; today, that number is 63%. </p>

<p>Migrants, however, are <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/2024/08/19/geographic-spotlights-a-closer-look-at-4-migration-stories/">more likely to have a religious affiliation</a>: 87%, compared with 70% of all people in the United States. In Maine, for example, where I live, journalists have noted how <a href="https://www.mainepublic.org/arts-and-culture/2024-06-13/african-immigration-to-maine-fuels-boom-in-new-churches-bringing-distinct-forms-of-christianity">African migrants are reinvigorating churches</a>. And many <a href="https://www.patheos.com/blogs/anxiousbench/2021/09/the-2020-census-immigration-and-the-future-of-american-evangelicalism/">thriving migrant churches are evangelical</a>.</p>

<p>Looking toward the future, I believe these trends will continue to transform U.S. religion, which may affect politics as well. Many migrants I met, including green-card holders and asylum-seekers, hoped to eventually gain citizenship and be able to vote. Many attended church alongside their own children, born in the U.S. – future voters whose attitudes may be shaped by their parents’ experiences of both migration and faith.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766542/original/file-20261015-50-bsrdsg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C50%2C1024%2C576&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A sanctuary full of people, photographed from the back of the room." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766542/original/file-20261015-50-bsrdsg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C50%2C1024%2C576&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766542/original/file-20261015-50-bsrdsg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=396&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766542/original/file-20261015-50-bsrdsg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=396&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766542/original/file-20261015-50-bsrdsg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=396&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766542/original/file-20261015-50-bsrdsg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=498&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766542/original/file-20261015-50-bsrdsg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=498&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766542/original/file-20261015-50-bsrdsg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=498&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>I learned that evangelical migrants’ identity as “people of God” was central to their political views, as it is for their white, U.S.-born counterparts. Some of them believed Trump would restore the United States to its presumed destiny as an explicitly Christian nation. His policies about abortion, marriage and gender seemed to outweigh concerns about the risks his immigration policies posed to them and their families. Since the start of his second term, with its waves of <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/01/16/nx-s1-5675286/violent-incidents-involving-ice-raise-questions-about-their-training-and-use-of-force">sometimes violent</a> and aggressive <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/25/us/ice-surge-immigration-arrests.html">ICE raids</a>, detentions and deportations, I have wondered how they would assess the administration today.</p>

<p>Regardless of their political views, it is clear that migrants will continue to look to evangelical faith to cope with and make sense of their experiences in the United States. My research underscores the significant role evangelical faith plays in the life of growing numbers of migrants and the far-reaching impacts of such faith for U.S. society.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/286504/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Joe Raedle/Getty Images In October 2024, right before the presidential election, I had coffee with Kim, a Congolese asylum-seeker living in southern Maine
Our conversation quickly turned to politics, and I cautiously asked about her views, although she could not vote
During his campaign, Donald Trump had vowed mass deportations , and I assumed immigration policies would be among her top priorities
But instead, she quickly turned to matters of faith, invoking her strongly held beliefs

Kim – a pseudonym, like all names used in this article – was an evangelical Christian whose life revolved around her church: a nondenominational congregation led by other Congolese migrants. “Democrats are not people of God,” she declared
People in her community were “traditional,” she added, and generally wanted politicians who were, too
Congolese Christians, she said, usually believed marriage should only occur between a man and a woman, that sex and gender are chosen by God, and that life is sacred from conception
Her pronouncement underscores an important but often overlooked reality
Popular commentary in the U.S. often portrays evangelicals as one homogeneous, overwhelmingly white group
In reality, they are diverse, from political views and geography to race: 3 in 10 U.S. evangelicals are not white
And a growing percentage are migrants – a term I use for people who have come to the U.S., regardless of their legal status
Belonging and belief Overall, 12% of evangelicals in the U.S. were born outside the country, according to a 2024 study conducted by the Pew Research Center
Another 7% have at least one parent born outside the country
These figures are likely underestimates, since undocumented migrants generally avoid surveys for fear of deportation
As an anthropologist of religion , I’ve studied the growing number of migrants drawn to evangelical faith – and learned how significantly faith shapes their lives in the United States
In turn, these migrants are shaping America’s religious landscape
Parishioners pray during a service at New Life Fellowship Church, which has many members from Liberia, in Euless, Texas, in 2014
Joe Raedle/Getty Images While writing my 2022 book, “ In the Hands of God ,” I spent over a year attending evangelical churches around Washington, D.C., that catered to Brazilian migrants
I interviewed about 80 churchgoers and surveyed dozens more
Congregants described how belief and belonging helped them overcome challenges such as loneliness, “feeling stuck” due to their legal precariousness and being exploited at work
I heard stories of employers holding migrants’ passports hostage, or refusing to pay construction workers seriously injured on the job
Migrants often told me that their churches’ close-knit communities, and evangelical Christianity’s emphasis on fostering an intimate relationship with God, gave them a sense of empowerment
Through prayer, worship, Bible study and fasting, they tried to discern and implement God’s plan for their lives
The three congregations that I attended offered multiple prayer, study and worship opportunities for migrants throughout the week, both at church and at congregants’ homes
Many pastors were migrants themselves and shared from the pulpit their stories of overcoming adversity

Gláucia, an undocumented migrant from Brazil, described leaving herself “in the hands of God” as she faced uncertainty about her future. “I love living here,” she explained. “But if God wants me to leave, I’m under God’s will
Therefore, I don’t get worried, because we can’t become worried about what comes tomorrow
Because tomorrow belongs to God. "The most I can do,” she added, “which I always try to do, is pray to God to give direction” to political leaders
Members of the First Brazilian Church of Boston pray during a Sunday evening service in 2013
Kelvin Ma/MediaNews Group/Boston Herald via Getty Images Growing communities Some people I met identified as evangelical before coming to the U.S., but a significant number were converts

Even among people who had attended evangelical churches in Brazil, many insisted that they truly “met Jesus” in the United States and reflected that their faith back home had been “lukewarm.” Angela, an undocumented migrant, knew many evangelicals in Brazil
It wasn’t until arriving in the U.S., though, that she converted from Catholicism
She told me, “When you are here, without your family, without any friends, you feel alone, and look for something to hold on to,” she told me
According to large-scale surveys, most immigrants in the U.S. are Christian , and the majority of Christian migrants are Catholic
Over the past several decades, however, a growing percentage of people in Latin America, long a Catholic stronghold, have been embracing evangelical churches
That has influenced the religious makeup of migrants to the United States
Others convert to evangelical Christianity once they arrive , as my research highlights
People attend Sunday services at the Church of Grace to Fujianese in New York in 2010

Najlah Feanny/Corbis via Getty Images Most of the migrants I met reported intense psychological pain as they endured family separation, workplace exploitation and legal uncertainty, which prompted them to search for meaning and comfort in religious spaces

<title>Treating depression during pregnancy may benefit baby’s brain development – new research</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764039/original/file-20261006-50-sc67av.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C6720%2C4480&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Depression affects 1 in 5 women during pregnancy. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/pregnant-woman-receiving-emotional-support-during-royalty-free-image/2229743179">SDI Productions/E+ via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Treating pregnant women’s depression with a short course of talk therapy doesn’t just improve their health – it can also shape <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78276-4">how their babies’ brains develop before birth</a>. That’s the finding of a new study we co-authored, published in the journal Nature Communications.  </p>

<p>The study is part of <a href="https://careprojectdenver.org/">an ongoing research project</a> that explores how a form of brief interpersonal psychotherapy called MOMCare, which is specially tailored to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/da.22405">treating prenatal depression</a>, affects pregnant women with depression and their babies. MOMCare consists of eight 50-minute sessions focused on building interpersonal skills, reducing conflict and strengthening social support. </p>

<p>We enrolled 234 pregnant women who reported having symptoms of depression during their routine prenatal care appointments. Mothers joined the research project during the first or second trimester and were randomly assigned to one of two groups. </p>

<p>Women in one group received MOMCare. Women in the other group received education about mental health, strategies for managing depression symptoms and referrals to mental health support services, such as therapy, in the community. Both groups continued getting their usual medical care, which could also include referrals to therapy or medication.</p>

<p>In a previous publication, we found that 36% of moms enrolled in our study were diagnosed with depression in pregnancy before getting MOMCare and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2023.0702">just 6% after it</a>, showing the intervention was effective. Women who received the MOMCare intervention were also more likely to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eclinm.2024.102601">carry their baby to term</a>, which is linked with shorter hospital stays after birth and improvements in many aspects of child health and development, including <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2020.2027">better school performance</a>. </p>

<p>In the current study, to investigate how this form of talk therapy affects a baby’s developing brain, we measured the volume of different brain areas using an imaging technique called <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diagnostics/4876-magnetic-resonance-imaging-mri">magnetic resonance imaging</a>, or MRI, within a few weeks of birth. We found that a brain area called the <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/hippocampus">hippocampus</a>, which plays a role in learning, memory and <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-is-emotional-regulation-a-child-psychologist-explains-280443">emotional regulation</a>, was 5% smaller by volume in infants whose mothers received MOMCare compared to mothers in the other group. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764079/original/file-20261006-50-msh4ky.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A baby in a high chair playing with an educational block toy" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764079/original/file-20261006-50-msh4ky.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764079/original/file-20261006-50-msh4ky.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764079/original/file-20261006-50-msh4ky.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764079/original/file-20261006-50-msh4ky.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764079/original/file-20261006-50-msh4ky.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764079/original/file-20261006-50-msh4ky.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764079/original/file-20261006-50-msh4ky.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Brain imaging showed a difference in the brains of newborns whose moms got talk therapy compared to those whose moms who did not.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/asian-baby-boy-develops-fine-motor-skills-playing-royalty-free-image/2232215754">travelism/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>



<p>Six months later, we brought the babies back into the lab to examine their emotional responses to unfamiliar experiences, such as encountering a noisy toy robot that danced and moved unpredictably. According to earlier studies, babies who respond more negatively to these tasks have higher levels of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/abn0000769">depression and anxiety</a> in adolescence. </p>

<p>In our study, we found that babies with a smaller hippocampal volume at birth tended to respond less negatively than those with larger volume. </p>

<p>It may seem counterintuitive that a smaller brain volume is associated with stronger emotional regulation, particularly since in adults smaller brain volume is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/nn958">often associated with negative effects</a>. However, in infancy the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2024.101392">brain is growing</a>, and faster growth may not always be advantageous. For example, one hypothesis proposes that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cobeha.2015.11.018">stress can accelerate early brain development</a>. </p>

<h2>Why it matters</h2>

<p>Depression affects up to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1377/hlthaff.2021.00615">1 in 5 women during pregnancy</a>. It also raises the risk of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/archgenpsychiatry.2010.111">pregnancy complications</a> such as high blood pressure and preterm birth. And having depression during pregnancy raises the risk of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lanepe.2026.101595">mental illness in the child</a>. </p>

<p>Pregnancy offers a unique opportunity to simultaneously improve the health of both mother and baby. This is because women often have more contact with the healthcare system during pregnancy than at other times in their lives. Treating a woman’s depression during her pregnancy benefits <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0954579418000470">two generations</a>, improving the health of the mother and her developing baby. </p>

<p>Even though both MOMCare and the control condition in our study provided more support than pregnant women experiencing symptoms of depression often receive, we still saw a big difference between the groups. This suggests that a targeted intervention, even a noninvasive and relatively low-cost one such as MOMCare, can make a big difference. </p>

<p>Our study is the first to show that treating a woman’s depression during pregnancy may influence infant brain development. It aligns with a small but growing number of randomized clinical trials showing that reducing maternal depression has benefits for babies, including improved <a href="https://doi.org/10.3368/jhr.1222-12693R3">emotional development</a> and changes in <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ssmmh.2022.100082">stress-related hormones</a>.</p>

<p>These findings, if confirmed, could explain the biological underpinnings behind why treating prenatal depression is so critical. Further, they support public health initiatives to increase <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cct.2025.107988">accessible mental health support</a> during pregnancy. </p>

<h2>What’s still unknown</h2>

<p>It’s not clear how lessening mom’s depression in pregnancy leads to changes in the baby’s brain. It’s possible, for example, that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.psyneuen.2016.10.005">stress-related hormones</a> or <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0033291719001909">inflammation associated with depression</a> could influence brain growth.</p>

<p>Another open question is how the brain changes we observed might affect babies’ development long term. We hope to address this by continuing to follow mothers and babies through early childhood. By tracking conditions such as depression and anxiety as the children get older, we hope to determine whether treating mothers’ depression in pregnancy has lasting benefits for their children’s mental health and well-being.</p>

title: Fentanyl is fueling overdose deaths in Colorado – what voters need to know about Proposition 132’s attempt to stiffen penalties

<title>Fentanyl is fueling overdose deaths in Colorado – what voters need to know about Proposition 132’s attempt to stiffen penalties</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763959/original/file-20261005-50-zotpy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5616%2C3744&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Fentanyl-related overdose deaths are a concern in Colorado.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/drug-grams-and-tabs-royalty-free-image/482857483?phrase=group%20of%20people%20fentanyl&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm">KatarzynaBialasiewicz/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Colorado continues to face an increase in overdose deaths while other states have seen a downturn.</p>

<p>Illicitly manufactured fentanyl, a potent opioid, emerged in the Colorado drug market around 2018. That was nearly five years after it began tormenting people who use street drugs in <a href="http://dx.doi.org/10.15585/mmwr.mm6614a2">Northeastern states</a>. </p>

<p>By 2019, fentanyl replaced other drugs as the <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/vsrr/drug-overdose-data.htm">driving force behind opioid overdoses in Colorado</a>, and it has <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/vsrr/drug-overdose-data.htm">held its grip</a> ever since.</p>

<p>But while <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/vsrr/drug-overdose-data.htm">overdose deaths in the U.S.</a> are currently experiencing a historic decline of almost 14%, Colorado is <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/state-watch/5878575-drug-overdose-deaths-declined-last-year-except-in-these-8-states/">one of eight states where rates are not dropping</a>. In fact, Colorado has had an increase of <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/vsrr/drug-overdose-data.htm">nearly 12% in overdose deaths</a> since April 2025. </p>

<p>Overdoses are top of mind for many everyday Coloradans, healthcare professionals, elected officials and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=WaGmzxoAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">public health experts like me</a>. </p>

<p><a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Colorado_Proposition_132,_Penalties_for_Fentanyl_Sale_and_Possession_Initiative_(2026)">Proposition 132</a> attempts to address these concerns by stiffening legal penalties. A conservative policy organization called Advance Colorado collected the signatures to get the initiative on the November ballot.</p>

<p>The proposed change to Colorado law would make possession of any amount of fentanyl a felony, require a mandatory minimum eight-year prison sentence for distribution of any quantity of fentanyl, and eliminate some existing opportunities for reduced penalties. </p>

<p>Before Coloradans head to the polls, it is worth examining the state’s overdose trends and considering whether Proposition 132 is likely to solve the problem.</p>

<h2>A 2022 law already increased penalties</h2>

<p>Let’s start by looking at Colorado’s past attempts to stop drug overdoses through legislation.</p>

<p>In recent years, the state has pursued some public health interventions but has leaned heavily on increasing criminal penalties for using and possessing fentanyl. </p>

<p>The 2022 <a href="https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb22-1326">Fentanyl Accountability and Prevention Act (HB22-1326)</a>, for instance, represented a major expansion of criminal penalties.</p>

<p>This law rolled back a <a href="https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb19-1263">2019 law</a> that had decriminalized small amounts of drugs. Specifically, HB22-1326 made the knowing possession of more than 1 gram and up to 4 grams of a <a href="https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb22-1326">substance containing fentanyl a Level 4 drug felony</a> punishable by up to 180 days in jail and two years of probation. </p>

<p>Unlike Proposition 132, the 2022 fentanyl act directed funding for the distribution of naloxone, an overdose reversal medication, and fentanyl test strips that help people identify fentanyl in their drugs before using them. Both <a href="https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.f174">naloxone</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.10077">fentanyl test strips</a> decrease the risk of fatal overdose. </p>

<p>The law did not direct funding toward evidence-based treatments such as methadone or buprenorphine for <a href="https://nida.nih.gov/research-topics/medications-opioid-use-disorder#buprenorphine">opioid use disorder</a>. </p>

<p><a href="https://patch.com/colorado/across-co/fentanyl-accountability-prevention-bill-moves-governors-desk">Supporters argued</a> that the legislation was necessary to prevent overdose deaths and get people treatment.</p>

<p>I led a research team that included addiction treatment providers and substance use–focused epidemiologists to study the effects of HB22-1326. Although more people were arrested and faced the tougher penalties, we found <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.drugpo.2025.105037">no increase in people beginning or staying on buprenorphine</a>. We also found that fewer people were starting and staying on methadone following the implementation of the law. </p>

<p>Importantly, we found that the law did not change <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamahealthforum.2025.2654">the trajectory of overdose deaths</a> compared to what was expected. Taken together, we found no substantial evidence that increasing criminal penalties, even with some increased funding for naloxone and overdose prevention, “saved lives” as proponents had hoped. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763966/original/file-20261005-50-xvc7lw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Top view of youth talking with a therapist while sitting in a circle during a meeting." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763966/original/file-20261005-50-xvc7lw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763966/original/file-20261005-50-xvc7lw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763966/original/file-20261005-50-xvc7lw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763966/original/file-20261005-50-xvc7lw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763966/original/file-20261005-50-xvc7lw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763966/original/file-20261005-50-xvc7lw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763966/original/file-20261005-50-xvc7lw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">In addition to increased criminalization, Colorado has invested in prevention programs and treatment support for users of illicit drugs.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/top-view-on-difficult-youth-talking-with-therapist-royalty-free-image/1007209056">KatarzynaBialasiewicz/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Colorado is already <a href="https://www.networkforphl.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/State-Fentanyl-Penalty-Enhancements_A-Comprehensive-Legal-Review-2.pdf">uniquely punitive toward people who use illicit drugs</a>, with some of the harshest penalties for drug possession and distribution in the U.S. Colorado’s public health response has developed alongside, not in place of, a substantial criminal-legal response.</p>

<h2>What decreases overdose deaths?</h2>

<p>Even with <a href="https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/HB24-1037">efforts to provide additional access to harm-reduction protections</a>, escalating criminal penalties have not produced the treatment gains or decreases in overdose deaths in Colorado that proponents promised. </p>

<p>So, let’s look at a place in the state where overdose deaths are actually falling to see what is being done differently there. </p>

<p>Larimer County, home of Colorado State University and part of Rocky Mountain National Park, offers the clearest contrast to the rest of the state. Accidental overdose deaths <a href="https://cohealthviz.dphe.state.co.us/t/HealthInformaticsPublic/views/Drug_Overdose_Dashboard_All_Years_No_Race_FINAL/Story1">have declined year after year since 2022</a>, down nearly 42% from 2021.</p>

<p>What’s going on in Larimer County?</p>

<p>For one, the Larimer County Jail is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s40352-026-00434-z">one of less than half</a> of the Colorado county jails that offers  that includes medications for opioid use disorder. </p>

<p>The sheriff’s office, in collaboration with several community-based organizations, has also flooded the community with naloxone through the <a href="https://www.larimer.gov/spotlights/2024/01/29/grant-fuels-battle-against-opioid-crisis-repeat-offenses">Reversal Project</a>. Furthermore, <a href="https://www.larimer.gov/bocc/regional-opioid-abatement-council#docaccess-d2eae7271383f0388efc8934636fbb8d">using opioid abatement funds</a>, the county has expanded youth and family support services, co-responder units and other harm-reduction services. The county has also steadily <a href="https://cohealthviz.dphe.state.co.us/t/PSDVIP-MHPPUBLIC/views/BuprenorphineDashboard/BupeNaive?%3Aembed=y&amp;%3AisGuestRedirectFromVizportal=y&amp;%3Aorigin=card_share_link">increased the number of people on buprenorphine</a>. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Naloxone can quickly reverse an opioid overdose.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/naloxone-kit-with-a-couple-of-vials-at-pharmacy-royalty-free-image/1361636220">Marvin Samuel Tolentino Pineda/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>No single intervention can be credited with Larimer County’s decline in accidental overdoes deaths. Criminal enforcement remains one component of the county’s response. Yet, what stands out is its emphasis on evidence-based interventions with an emphasis on expanding treatment access and harm-reduction services that save lives and give people the stability and opportunity to build healthier lives. </p>

<h2>A polysubstance problem</h2>

<p>In addition, Proposition 132 has a major flaw. It targets one drug: fentanyl. </p>

<p>But the <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/overdose-prevention/data-research/facts-stats/sudors-dashboard-fatal-overdose-data.html">available data suggests</a> most people take fentanyl together with stimulants such as methamphetamine. Both drugs can be fatal.</p>

<p>Between 2020 and 2024, nearly 40% of <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/overdose-prevention/data-research/facts-stats/sudors-dashboard-fatal-overdose-data.html">overdose deaths in Colorado</a> involved both opioids and stimulants. </p>

<p>National figures follow a similar pattern. Nationally, 43% of overdose deaths in 2024 <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/overdose-prevention/data-research/facts-stats/sudors-dashboard-fatal-overdose-data.html">involved both opioids and stimulants</a>. </p>

<p>Targeting one substance, as Proposition 132 does, ignores the fact that the state has a true “polysubstance” epidemic and will end up making people who unknowingly possess fentanyl susceptible to harsher penalties set forth by Proposition 132.</p>

<p>Since Colorado increased fentanyl penalties in 2022, the promised treatment gains examined in our research have not materialized. The state’s number of overdoses has continued to climb.</p>

<p>Those facts do not mean that criminal penalties alone caused Colorado’s worsening trend. But they do raise an important question as voters consider Proposition 132: What evidence suggests that increasing those penalties further will address the rise in overdose deaths?</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292870/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Pennsylvania’s aging prisons weren’t built for today’s extreme weather – leaving women and seniors especially at risk of illness and death</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765016/original/file-20261008-60-aap6mb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3500%2C2333&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">People in prison can&#39;t just switch on the air conditioning when it starts to swelter.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/exterior-view-of-chester-county-prison-from-which-convicted-news-photo/1657117984">Mark Makela/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>When outdoor temperatures spike to 103 degrees Fahrenheit (39 degrees Celsius), or drop to -9 F (-23 C), like they did across Pennsylvania last year, people locked up in jails and prisons cannot simply turn on the air conditioning or find a public warming center.</p>

<p>For several years, people in custody, advocates and local media <a href="https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2024/07/pennsylvania-prisons-air-conditioning-heatwave">have sounded the alarm</a> about the dangers posed by extreme temperatures in Pennsylvania’s state prisons. </p>

<p>Conditions inside Pennsylvania’s prisons have been described <a href="https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2024/07/pennsylvania-prisons-air-conditioning-heatwave">as a sauna</a> during a summer heat wave and bitterly cold in the winter, especially when heating systems have malfunctioned. Amy McBride, a woman in her early 60s incarcerated at MCI Muncy, <a href="https://prisonjournalismproject.org/2025/02/25/extreme-cold-prison/">told the Prison Journalism Project</a>, “I tend to wear two to three layers of pants and four to six layers of shirts (in winter), sometimes with my jacket and coat over them.” </p>

<p>I am an epidemiologist who <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&amp;user=rhfnW0YAAAAJ&amp;view_op=list_works&amp;sortby=pubdate">studies the health of incarcerated people</a>. My colleagues and I put numbers to these warnings in a recent study. We found that extreme hot and cold temperatures were associated with <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78012-y">higher rates of deaths, infirmary admissions and transfers to external medical facilities</a> among imprisoned people in Pennsylvania over the past 20 years. </p>

<p>While these temperature hazards are not unique to Pennsylvania, several factors make this issue a particular concern for the state. Pennsylvania has the nation’s <a href="https://bjs.ojp.gov/library/publications/prisoners-2023-statistical-tables">sixth-largest prison population</a> among U.S. states. Nearly 40,000 people are confined in Pennsylvania prisons. </p>

<p>Furthermore, most of Pennsylvania’s state prison facilities were built in the 1990s or earlier, when weather patterns were not so <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dep/residents/climate-change/impacts">extreme</a>. Some, including the state correctional institutions in <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/cor/state-prisons/sci-cambridge-springs">Cambridge Springs</a>, <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/cor/state-prisons/sci-dallas">Dallas</a>, <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/cor/state-prisons/sci-laurel-highlands">Laurel Highlands</a>, <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/cor/state-prisons/sci-muncy">Muncy</a>, <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/cor/state-prisons/sci-waymart">Waymart</a> and <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/cor/state-prisons/sci-huntingdon">Huntingdon</a>, the oldest continuously running correctional facility in Pennsylvania, have partial or very limited air conditioning. This means they have air conditioning in some buildings or units, such as nursing care areas, and not others.</p>

<p>Previous research also suggests that while hot temperatures <a href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0281389">pose risks to incarcerated people across the country</a>, those incarcerated in the Northeast have experienced some of the greatest increases in heat-related mortality risk since 2001.</p>

<h2>Prison healthcare systems under strain</h2>

<p>Even under normal weather conditions, prison healthcare systems are highly strained. People in prison are more likely than the general population to have <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2017.04.040">chronic medical conditions such as heart disease</a>, and the state’s prison population <a href="https://www.legis.state.pa.us/WU01/LI/TR/Transcripts/2024_0522_0002_TSTMNY.pdf">is getting older</a>, which increases its medical needs and expenses. The average age at prison admission has increased from 31 in 2000 to <a href="https://www.legis.state.pa.us/WU01/LI/TR/Transcripts/2024_0522_0002_TSTMNY.pdf">38 in 2023</a>.</p>

<p>The average cost for medications alone for adults over 50 in the state’s prison is <a href="https://www.legis.state.pa.us/WU01/LI/TR/Transcripts/2024_0522_0002_TSTMNY.pdf">US$3,357 per person per year</a>. That’s <a href="https://www.legis.state.pa.us/WU01/LI/TR/Transcripts/2024_0522_0002_TSTMNY.pdf">53% more</a> than costs for younger incarcerated adults. </p>

<p>The state prison system experiences <a href="https://www.legis.state.pa.us/WU01/LI/TR/Transcripts/2024_0522_0002_TSTMNY.pdf">chronic staffing shortages</a> of corrections officers, nurses and physicians. Some facilities have experienced vacancy rates of medical staff of nearly 40%. Shortages of corrections officers result in greater restrictions on the movement of incarcerated people, who then have less access to health appointments, group therapy and other programming. This can be especially difficult for <a href="https://prisonjournalismproject.org/2026/03/17/prison-staffing-problems-are-especially-hard-on-lifers/">older incarcerated people and those who have been incarcerated for long periods of time</a>, because they have greater medical needs and are often more isolated from loved ones.</p>

<p>Constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment <a href="https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/USREPORTS-429/USREPORTS-429-97">prohibit deliberate indifference to prisoners’ medical needs</a>. But in addition to staffing shortages and other administrative challenges with healthcare delivery in prisons, incarcerated people also face financial barriers. </p>

<p>In Pennsylvania, they must pay a <a href="https://www.pa.gov/content/dam/copapwp-pagov/en/cor/documents/about-us/doc-policies/820%20Co-Payment%20for%20Medical%20Services.pdf">$5 copay</a> per visit to receive medical treatment that is determined by the Department of Correction to not be an emergency. This may sound low but is substantial in the context of wages that range from <a href="https://www.prisonsociety.org/updates/doc-raises-wages-for-incarcerated-people">23 cents to 50 cents per hour</a>. </p>

<h2>Incarcerated women may face higher heat risks</h2>

<p>One unexpected finding from our analysis was that women in Pennsylvania state prisons experienced greater increases in rates of infirmary visits and transfers to external medical facilities on and after extremely hot days than men. </p>

<p>This was unexpected because <a href="https://www.doi.org/10.1097/EDE.0000000000000375">previous studies</a> haven’t consistently shown that women are more vulnerable to heat-related health risks. But these studies were conducted in the general population, not among people in prison.</p>

<p>Incarcerated people experience what medical researchers call “<a href="https://www.doi.org/10.1177/00221465211052568">accelerated aging</a>” because of the stressors they experience during and prior to incarceration. This means their biologic age is ahead of their chronological age. They are more likely to experience menopause, cancer and chronic disease <a href="https://whyy.org/articles/in-prison-women-develop-diseases-earlier-and-often/">at a younger age</a> than would typically be expected. </p>

<p>Hot flashes and night sweats are common symptoms of menopause that can become <a href="https://www.doi.org/10.1177/10783458261449636">life threatening</a> during extreme heat events and when cooling, hydration and hormone therapy are limited or unavailable. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Close up shot of healthcare worker's gloved hands handing blister pack of pills to person wearing orange" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764683/original/file-20261007-50-4cfh05.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C293%2C5616%2C3159&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764683/original/file-20261007-50-4cfh05.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764683/original/file-20261007-50-4cfh05.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764683/original/file-20261007-50-4cfh05.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764683/original/file-20261007-50-4cfh05.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764683/original/file-20261007-50-4cfh05.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764683/original/file-20261007-50-4cfh05.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Extreme heat can turn common symptoms of menopause into health hazards for women in prison.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/close-up-shot-of-healthcare-workers-gloved-hands-royalty-free-image/1397838530">Mindful Media/E+ Collection via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Preparing for a warmer climate</h2>

<p>Our research found that extreme heat and extreme cold increase the demands on an already strained system of prison operations and healthcare delivery. These demands will likely only get worse as extreme temperatures continue to intensify.</p>

<p>We believe climate resilience planning will require improvements in prison conditions, improvements in prison healthcare systems, and policy efforts to reduce the number of people – particularly older adults – who are incarcerated.</p>

excerpt: People in prison can't just switch on the air conditioning when it starts to swelter
body: People in prison can't just switch on the air conditioning when it starts to swelter

Mark Makela/Getty Images When outdoor temperatures spike to 103 degrees Fahrenheit (39 degrees Celsius), or drop to -9 F (-23 C), like they did across Pennsylvania last year, people locked up in jails and prisons cannot simply turn on the air conditioning or find a public warming center
For several years, people in custody, advocates and local media have sounded the alarm about the dangers posed by extreme temperatures in Pennsylvania’s state prisons
Conditions inside Pennsylvania’s prisons have been described as a sauna during a summer heat wave and bitterly cold in the winter, especially when heating systems have malfunctioned

Amy McBride, a woman in her early 60s incarcerated at MCI Muncy, told the Prison Journalism Project , “I tend to wear two to three layers of pants and four to six layers of shirts (in winter), sometimes with my jacket and coat over them.” I am an epidemiologist who studies the health of incarcerated people
My colleagues and I put numbers to these warnings in a recent study

We found that extreme hot and cold temperatures were associated with higher rates of deaths, infirmary admissions and transfers to external medical facilities among imprisoned people in Pennsylvania over the past 20 years
While these temperature hazards are not unique to Pennsylvania, several factors make this issue a particular concern for the state
Pennsylvania has the nation’s sixth-largest prison population among U.S. states
Nearly 40,000 people are confined in Pennsylvania prisons
Furthermore, most of Pennsylvania’s state prison facilities were built in the 1990s or earlier, when weather patterns were not so extreme

Some, including the state correctional institutions in Cambridge Springs , Dallas , Laurel Highlands , Muncy , Waymart and Huntingdon , the oldest continuously running correctional facility in Pennsylvania, have partial or very limited air conditioning
This means they have air conditioning in some buildings or units, such as nursing care areas, and not others

Previous research also suggests that while hot temperatures pose risks to incarcerated people across the country , those incarcerated in the Northeast have experienced some of the greatest increases in heat-related mortality risk since 2001
Prison healthcare systems under strain Even under normal weather conditions, prison healthcare systems are highly strained

People in prison are more likely than the general population to have chronic medical conditions such as heart disease , and the state’s prison population is getting older , which increases its medical needs and expenses
The average age at prison admission has increased from 31 in 2000 to 38 in 2023
The average cost for medications alone for adults over 50 in the state’s prison is US$3,357 per person per year
That’s 53% more than costs for younger incarcerated adults
The state prison system experiences chronic staffing shortages of corrections officers, nurses and physicians
Some facilities have experienced vacancy rates of medical staff of nearly 40%
Shortages of corrections officers result in greater restrictions on the movement of incarcerated people, who then have less access to health appointments, group therapy and other programming

This can be especially difficult for older incarcerated people and those who have been incarcerated for long periods of time , because they have greater medical needs and are often more isolated from loved ones
Constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment prohibit deliberate indifference to prisoners’ medical needs
But in addition to staffing shortages and other administrative challenges with healthcare delivery in prisons, incarcerated people also face financial barriers
In Pennsylvania, they must pay a $5 copay per visit to receive medical treatment that is determined by the Department of Correction to not be an emergency
This may sound low but is substantial in the context of wages that range from 23 cents to 50 cents per hour

Incarcerated women may face higher heat risks One unexpected finding from our analysis was that women in Pennsylvania state prisons experienced greater increases in rates of infirmary visits and transfers to external medical facilities on and after extremely hot days than men
This was unexpected because previous studies haven’t consistently shown that women are more vulnerable to heat-related health risks
But these studies were conducted in the general population, not among people in prison
Incarcerated people experience what medical researchers call “ accelerated aging ” because of the stressors they experience during and prior to incarceration
This means their biologic age is ahead of their chronological age
They are more likely to experience menopause, cancer and chronic disease at a younger age than would typically be expected
Hot flashes and night sweats are common symptoms of menopause that can become life threatening during extreme heat events and when cooling, hydration and hormone therapy are limited or unavailable
Extreme heat can turn common symptoms of menopause into health hazards for women in prison

Mindful Media/E+ Collection via Getty Images Preparing for a warmer climate Our research found that extreme heat and extreme cold increase the demands on an already strained system of prison operations and healthcare delivery
These demands will likely only get worse as extreme temperatures continue to intensify

We believe climate resilience planning will require improvements in prison conditions, improvements in prison healthcare systems, and policy efforts to reduce the number of people – particularly older adults – who are incarcerated

title: How to lose a job in five days
excerpt: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia speaks during a news briefing at the White House on October 13, 2026. | Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images This story appe
body: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia speaks during a news briefing at the White House on October 13, 2026. | Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia is out of a job after only five days.  What happened? Zacharia was fired on Friday after less than a week in her new role, after a rocky start that included a halting performance in the briefing room, a scandal over her legal credentials, and a round of less-than-successful cleanup interviews .  The firing makes her the shortest-tenured White House press secretary in history, outstripping even first-term Trump communications director Anthony Scaramucci, who made it 10 or 11 days (figures vary) before getting the boot.  “Records are made to be broken,” Scaramucci posted on Friday . “But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.” (No word yet on whether the “Zacharia” will emerge as a unit of time, as the “Scaramucci” has.)  What’s the context? Zacharia’s remarkably short stint behind the podium unfolded as the White House is engaged in an unprecedented attack on press freedom: The administration is still trying to ban three media outlets — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from the White House, though as of earlier this week, a judge is still blocking the ban from taking effect

The diminished nature of the press secretary job was on full display in Zacharia’s sole briefing on Tuesday , when she took questions from just three outlets: Breitbart, Fox News, and the Daily Mail.  Why does this matter? Zacharia’s no good, very bad week is not likely to leave much of a lasting mark in its own right — other than, perhaps, as pub trivia — but as NBC’s Garrett Haake points out , it’s a very tangible manifestation of a White House that seems to have no idea how to spin itself out of crisis with just weeks until the midterm elections.  Most recently, Trump has landed on flat-out lying about the state of the economy — but like Zacharia’s time as press secretary, it doesn’t seem like it’s going to go all that well

And with that, it’s time to log off… The underlying trend — municipal inaction — may be infuriating, but I loved this story about “tactical urbanism” from my colleague Sara Herschander.  As she writes, vigilante activists have taken to painting their own crosswalks, building benches, and even installing makeshift bike lanes in their neighborhoods — and every time they do, “they remind us that it is not actually that hard — or even that expensive — to do many of the simple things that can make our cities safer and more pleasant places to live.”  You can read Sara’s full piece here , no gift link needed
Enjoy, have a great weekend, and we’ll see you on Monday!

title: West Bank settlers brutally attack a Washington Post journalist
excerpt: Photojournalist Heidi Levine is transferred on a stretcher into an ambulance after she was attacked by Israeli settlers while photographing Palestinian farmers
body: Photojournalist Heidi Levine is transferred on a stretcher into an ambulance after she was attacked by Israeli settlers while photographing Palestinian farmers harvesting their olives on October 16, 2026. | Ahmad Gharabli/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day
On Friday, Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians living in the West Bank, as well as a Washington Post photographer, who was hospitalized with serious injuries
Photojournalist Heidi Levine was knocked down, beaten, and robbed of her camera equipment by masked settlers in an attack captured on video by other journalists
Those other members of the press rescued her from the attackers while Israel Defense Forces soldiers reportedly stood by
Levine had lacerations and a wound to her hand that split her finger to the bone, according to the Post , which condemned the attack in a statement
Jasper Nathaniel, an independent journalist who helped Levine escape the attack, said that Levine also had cracked ribs, and may have been stabbed
Assaults like this one are becoming more common in the West Bank, where settler violence — which is currently targeting the ongoing olive harvest — has worsened

Last week, another photojournalist for the news wire Agence France-Presse was beaten with rifles by settlers, and Palestinian residents of the West Bank have been shot, beaten, and terrorized while the Israeli settlers targeting them face few consequences
Why settler violence is growing in the West Bank As my colleague Zack Beauchamp recently explained, under international law, the settler movement in the West Bank is clearly illegal
Nevertheless, it’s continued to grow, and it has a friend in the current Israeli government led by Benjamin Netanyahu

It’s also becoming increasingly violent.  Two current Israeli officials, Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben Gvir, are settlers themselves, and both have used their offices — as ministers of finance and national security, respectively — to  further the settler cause , including by making it easier for settlers to commit unchecked violence against Palestinians.  The United Nations  reported in June that settler attacks had reached “the highest sustained levels ever recorded…with [an average of] six daily attacks that have resulted in casualties, property damage or both,” and in many Palestinians being forced from their homes by settlers

In late September , the International Committee of the Red Cross said that expanding Israeli settlements and violence by settlers was “making everyday life untenable” for Palestinian residents of the West Bank

As Zack has reported , settlements and settler violence are both intentional tactics, serving to force more Palestinians off their land, isolate the ones who stay, and push any potential two-state solution further out of reach.  That kind of violence is likely only to worsen in the weeks to come: Israel will hold elections on October 27, which could well result in Netanyahu’s settler-friendly government losing power
As a result, the Washington Post reported earlier this month , settlers are “racing to lock down gains” before the election with ever more extreme violence
One link for later ➨ Agentified kind of life
My colleague Adam Clark Estes turned the keys to his life over to a passel of AI agents for two weeks to see what would happen

They successfully saved him some times, he writes, largely with mundane tasks — but he left with mixed feelings about the experiment, including the possibility of contributing to a world with more AI slop

Before you go… Did you know… that the aerodynamic crouch used by jockeys in horse racing — known as the “martini glass position” — made race times roughly 5 to 7 percent faster ? Jockeys maintain it with only a few toes resting on each stirrup
